name: Robbins Ch. 3 — Inflammation and Repair
description: Pathology MCQs and short-answer questions covering Robbins & Cotran Chapter 3, in chapter order.

cards.front:
Inflammation is best defined in the provided text as a response of:

A. All tissues that delivers antibodies to lymph nodes
B. Vascularized tissues that deliver leukocytes and host-defense molecules from the circulation to sites of infection and cell damage
C. Avascular tissues that eliminate toxins by fibrosis
D. Epithelial tissues that prevent all microbial entry
cards.back:
B — Vascularized tissues that deliver leukocytes and host-defense molecules from the circulation to sites of infection and cell damage

Robbins defines inflammation as a response of vascularized tissues that brings leukocytes and host-defense molecules to sites of infection or cell damage.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Which statement regarding inflammation is correct?

A. It is inherently harmful and usually unnecessary for survival
B. It is primarily a manifestation of autoimmune disease
C. It is a protective response essential for survival
D. It is a response limited to infectious organisms
cards.back:
C — It is a protective response essential for survival

Although the term often implies harm in common usage, Robbins emphasizes that inflammation is protective and essential for survival.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Inflammation helps rid the host of:

A. Only the initial cause of injury
B. Only necrotic tissue
C. Both the initial cause of injury and the consequences of injury
D. Only extracellular microbes
cards.back:
C — Both the initial cause of injury and the consequences of injury

Examples of the initial causes are microbes and toxins; consequences include necrotic cells and tissues.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT listed as a mediator/component of host defense in the introductory definition?

A. Phagocytic leukocytes
B. Antibodies
C. Complement proteins
D. Fibroblasts
cards.back:
D — Fibroblasts

The introductory passage specifically names phagocytic leukocytes, antibodies, and complement proteins as mediators of defense.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Most leukocytes involved in inflammation normally:

A. Remain permanently in tissues
B. Circulate in a resting state in blood and can be rapidly recruited
C. Remain inside lymph nodes
D. Circulate only during infection
cards.back:
B — Circulate in a resting state in blood and can be rapidly recruited

The text states that many inflammatory cells normally circulate in a resting state and can rapidly be recruited to sites throughout the body.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Some inflammatory cells that reside in tissues function primarily as:

A. Antibody-producing cells
B. Fibroblasts
C. Sentinels for threats
D. Platelet precursors
cards.back:
C — Sentinels for threats

Tissue-resident inflammatory cells act as sentinels, detecting potential threats before recruitment of circulating cells.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
According to the text, in the absence of inflammation:

A. Infections may go unchecked and wounds may fail to heal
B. Fibrosis is completely prevented
C. Leukocyte apoptosis is prevented
D. All tissue injury resolves spontaneously
cards.back:
A — Infections may go unchecked and wounds may fail to heal

Robbins states that without inflammation, infections would go unchecked, wounds would never heal, and injured tissues might remain as persistent festering sores.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
The suffix “-itis” after an organ denotes:

A. Malignancy
B. Necrosis
C. Inflammation at that site
D. Autoimmunity
cards.back:
C — Inflammation at that site

Examples given include appendicitis, conjunctivitis, and meningitis.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Which sequence correctly represents the “five R’s” of the inflammatory response?

A. Recognition → repair → recruitment → removal → regulation
B. Recruitment → recognition → removal → regulation → repair
C. Recognition → recruitment → removal → regulation → repair
D. Recognition → removal → recruitment → repair → regulation
cards.back:
C — Recognition → recruitment → removal → regulation → repair

The Robbins summary describes the five R's as recognition, recruitment, removal, regulation, and repair.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
The major participants in the inflammatory reaction in tissues are:

A. Platelets and fibroblasts
B. Blood vessels and leukocytes
C. Lymph nodes and antibodies
D. Mast cells and fibroblasts
cards.back:
B — Blood vessels and leukocytes

The text identifies blood vessels and leukocytes as the major participants.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
During inflammation, blood vessels primarily respond by:

A. Constricting and decreasing permeability
B. Dilating and increasing permeability
C. Thrombosing immediately
D. Preventing leukocyte attachment
cards.back:
B — Dilating and increasing permeability

These changes permit selected circulating proteins to enter the site of infection or tissue damage.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Activated recruited leukocytes acquire the ability to destroy all of the following EXCEPT:

A. Microbes
B. Dead cells
C. Foreign bodies
D. Normal host tissue exclusively
cards.back:
D — Normal host tissue exclusively

Leukocytes ingest and destroy microbes, dead cells, foreign bodies, and unwanted materials; injury to normal tissue is an adverse consequence, not their primary target.

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front: Define inflammation.
cards.back:
Inflammation is a response of vascularized tissues that delivers leukocytes and host- defense molecules from the circulation to sites of infection and cell damage to eliminate offending agents.

Key points:
• Vascularized tissue response
• Recruitment from circulation
• Leukocytes and host-defense molecules
• Infection/cell damage
• Elimination of offending agents

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front: What are the five R’s of inflammation?
cards.back:
Recognition, recruitment, removal, regulation, and repair.

Key points:
• Recognition of injurious agent
• Recruitment of leukocytes
• Removal of agent
• Regulation/termination
• Repair/resolution

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front: What are the major components of the inflammatory response?
cards.back:
The major components are the vascular reaction and cellular response, principally involving blood vessels and leukocytes.

Key points:
• Blood vessels
• Leukocytes
• Increased vascular permeability
• Leukocyte adhesion/migration
• Activated leukocyte function

— Overview of inflammation: definitions and general features

cards.front:
Acute inflammation typically develops:

A. Over months
B. Within minutes or hours
C. Only after chronic inflammation
D. Only after 1–2 weeks
cards.back:
B — Within minutes or hours

Acute inflammation usually begins within minutes or hours and lasts several hours to a few days.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
The predominant leukocytes in typical acute inflammation are:

A. Lymphocytes
B. Plasma cells
C. Neutrophils
D. Eosinophils
cards.back:
C — Neutrophils

Acute inflammation is characterized by emigration of leukocytes, predominantly neutrophils.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Which combination best describes chronic inflammation?

A. Minutes to hours; neutrophils; little fibrosis
B. Longer duration; more tissue destruction; fibrosis
C. Several hours; no tissue injury
D. Rapid resolution; only vascular changes
cards.back:
B — Longer duration; more tissue destruction; fibrosis

Chronic inflammation lasts longer and is associated with increased tissue destruction and scarring/fibrosis.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Chronic inflammation may:

A. Only arise de novo
B. Only follow acute inflammation
C. Follow acute inflammation or arise de novo
D. Never coexist with acute inflammation
cards.back:
C — Follow acute inflammation or arise de novo

Robbins explicitly states both possibilities.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Which is an example of chronic inflammation coexisting with unresolved acute inflammation?

A. Asthma
B. Peptic ulcer
C. Myocardial infarction
D. Frostbite
cards.back:
B — Peptic ulcer

Peptic ulcers are specifically cited as an example where chronic inflammation may coexist with unresolved acute inflammation.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Celsus first described which four cardinal signs of inflammation?

A. Rubor, tumor, calor, dolor
B. Dolor, pallor, tumor, edema
C. Calor, cyanosis, rubor, fibrosis
D. Tumor, necrosis, dolor, functio laesa
cards.back:
A — Rubor, tumor, calor, dolor

Celsus, a Roman writer of the first century AD, listed redness, swelling, heat, and pain.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Who added loss of function (functio laesa) as the fifth cardinal sign?

A. Celsus
B. John Hunter
C. Rudolf Virchow
D. Elie Metchnikoff
cards.back:
C — Rudolf Virchow

Virchow added loss of function in the 19th century.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
John Hunter stated in 1793 that inflammation:

A. Is always a disease
B. Is a stereotypic response with a salutary effect
C. Is caused exclusively by histamine
D. Is necessarily chronic
cards.back:
B — Is a stereotypic response with a salutary effect

Hunter emphasized that inflammation is not a disease, but a stereotypic host response with beneficial effects.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Elie Metchnikoff discovered phagocytosis by observing:

A. Bacterial toxins in human serum
B. Rose-thorn ingestion by starfish larvae amebocytes and bacterial ingestion by mammalian leukocytes
C. Histamine release from mast cells
D. Platelet aggregation
cards.back:
B — Rose-thorn ingestion by starfish larvae amebocytes and bacterial ingestion by mammalian leukocytes

This observation in the 1880s led to his concept that inflammation brings phagocytes to injured areas.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Sir Thomas Lewis established the concept that vascular changes of inflammation are mediated by:

A. Antibodies alone
B. Chemical substances such as histamine
C. Fibroblasts
D. Complement only
cards.back:
B — Chemical substances such as histamine

Lewis’s work in skin showed that locally produced chemical mediators such as histamine mediate vascular changes.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Which of the following is listed among the most common and medically important causes of inflammation?

A. Bacterial infection
B. Fibroblast proliferation
C. Angiogenesis
D. Collagen maturation
cards.back:
A — Bacterial infection

Infections and microbial toxins are among the most common and important causes.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
The outcome of infection-associated inflammation is determined largely by:

A. Pathogen type and host response
B. Age alone
C. Fibroblast number alone
D. Serum albumin alone
cards.back:
A — Pathogen type and host response

Robbins states that outcomes are determined largely by the type of pathogen and host response, with other host characteristics contributing.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Sepsis, as described in the provided text, is:

A. Local inflammation restricted to a wound
B. A systemic inflammatory reaction occurring in some disseminated bacterial infections
C. A chronic granulomatous disorder
D. A form of allergic inflammation only
cards.back:
B — A systemic inflammatory reaction occurring in some disseminated bacterial infections

Some disseminated bacterial infections produce systemic inflammatory reactions with widespread abnormalities, termed sepsis.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Which statement about inflammatory mediators is correct?

A. They are produced exclusively by leukocytes
B. They are soluble factors produced by cells or derived from plasma proteins
C. They are only activated after fibrosis
D. They determine only the duration of inflammation
cards.back:
B — They are soluble factors produced by cells or derived from plasma proteins

Mediators are produced by cells or derived from plasma proteins and are generated/activated in response to inflammatory stimuli.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Which of the following can trigger inflammatory mediator production according to Robbins?

A. Only bacteria
B. Microbes, necrotic cells, and hypoxia
C. Only viruses and fungi
D. Only tissue trauma
cards.back:
B — Microbes, necrotic cells, and hypoxia

Even hypoxia can trigger mediator elaboration and inflammation.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Acute and chronic inflammation were originally distinguished primarily by:

A. Type of pathogen
B. Duration
C. Histologic location
D. Amount of collagen
cards.back:
B — Duration

The original distinction was based on duration, although Robbins notes that they differ in several other ways.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
In Table 3.1, acute respiratory distress syndrome is associated with tissue injury involving predominantly:

A. Eosinophils
B. Neutrophils
C. Macrophages
D. Lymphocytes
cards.back:
B — Neutrophils

The table lists neutrophils for acute respiratory distress syndrome.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
In the provided table, acute asthma is associated with:

A. Neutrophils and complement
B. Eosinophils and IgE antibodies
C. Macrophages and fibroblasts
D. Cytokines only
cards.back:
B — Eosinophils and IgE antibodies

Table 3.1 specifically lists eosinophils and IgE antibodies.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Septic shock in Table 3.1 is associated principally with:

A. Cytokines
B. Eosinophils
C. Fibroblasts
D. Complement alone
cards.back:
A — Cytokines

The table associates septic shock with cytokines.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Which pairing is correctly matched?

A. Atherosclerosis — macrophages and lymphocytes
B. Pulmonary fibrosis — eosinophils and IgE
C. Arthritis — neutrophils only
D. Asthma — fibroblasts only
cards.back:
A — Atherosclerosis — macrophages and lymphocytes

Table 3.1 lists macrophages and lymphocytes in atherosclerosis and macrophages/fibroblasts in pulmonary fibrosis.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Which combination is correctly matched?

A. Acute — slow onset, monocytes
B. Acute — fast onset, mainly neutrophils
C. Chronic — fast onset, mainly neutrophils
D. Chronic — minutes to hours
cards.back:
B — Acute — fast onset, mainly neutrophils

Table 3.2 characterizes acute inflammation by onset in minutes/hours and predominantly neutrophilic infiltrates.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Compared with acute inflammation, chronic inflammation generally has:

A. Milder, self-limited tissue injury
B. More severe and progressive tissue injury and fibrosis
C. More prominent local/systemic signs
D. Faster onset
cards.back:
B — More severe and progressive tissue injury and fibrosis

The chronic pattern is associated with often severe, progressive tissue injury and fibrosis.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
Local and systemic signs are, according to Table 3.2:

A. More prominent in chronic inflammation
B. Prominent in acute and less so in chronic inflammation
C. Absent in acute inflammation
D. Identical in both
cards.back:
B — Prominent in acute and less so in chronic inflammation

That is the specific tabulated distinction.

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front: Compare acute and chronic inflammation.
cards.back:
Acute inflammation is rapid, usually self-limited, neutrophil-predominant, and often causes mild tissue injury; chronic inflammation is slower, longer-lasting, associated with mononuclear cells, and tends to produce more tissue destruction and fibrosis.

Key points:
• Acute: minutes/hours
• Chronic: days or longer
• Neutrophils vs monocytes/macrophages + lymphocytes
• Mild/self-limited vs severe/progressive injury
• Fibrosis more characteristic of chronic inflammation

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front: List the historical milestones mentioned in Robbins for inflammation.
cards.back:
Egyptian papyrus (~3000 BC); Celsus—four cardinal signs; Virchow—loss of function; John Hunter—beneficial stereotypic response; Metchnikoff—phagocytosis; Sir Thomas Lewis—chemical mediators such as histamine.

Key points:
• Celsus
• Virchow
• Hunter
• Metchnikoff
• Lewis
• Their specific contributions

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front: Enumerate the major causes of inflammation given in the chapter.
cards.back:
Infections/microbial toxins, tissue necrosis, foreign bodies, and immune reactions/hypersensitivity; trauma is also discussed as a mechanism of tissue injury.

Key points:
• Bacterial/viral/fungal/parasitic infections
• Microbial toxins
• Tissue necrosis
• Foreign bodies
• Immune/hypersensitivity reactions

— Acute vs chronic inflammation, historical highlights, and causes

cards.front:
The initiating step in inflammatory reactions is:

A. Fibrosis
B. Recognition of microbial components or substances released from damaged cells
C. Leukocyte apoptosis
D. Scar remodeling
cards.back:
B — Recognition of microbial components or substances released from damaged cells

Robbins explicitly identifies recognition as the initiating step.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Cellular receptors for microbes are located in all of the following compartments EXCEPT:

A. Plasma membrane
B. Endosomes
C. Cytosol
D. Golgi apparatus as the principal compartment described
cards.back:
D — Golgi apparatus as the principal compartment described

The text identifies plasma membrane receptors for extracellular microbes, endosomal receptors for ingested microbes, and cytosolic receptors for intracellular microbes.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Plasma membrane microbial receptors primarily sense:

A. Intracellular microbes
B. Extracellular microbes
C. Nuclear DNA
D. Fibrosis
cards.back:
B — Extracellular microbes

Plasma membrane receptors are described for sensing extracellular microbes.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Endosomal receptors are particularly relevant for:

A. Ingested microbes
B. Extracellular matrix proteins
C. Fibroblasts
D. Red blood cells
cards.back:
A — Ingested microbes

The text maps endosomal receptors to ingested microbes.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
The best-defined family of microbial-recognition receptors mentioned is:

A. Immunoglobulins
B. Toll-like receptors
C. Selectins
D. Integrins
cards.back:
B — Toll-like receptors

TLRs are described as the best-defined cellular receptors involved in microbial sensing.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
TLRs are expressed on all of the following cell types mentioned in the text EXCEPT:

A. Epithelial cells
B. Dendritic cells
C. Macrophages
D. Erythrocytes
cards.back:
D — Erythrocytes

The passage lists epithelial cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and other leukocytes.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Engagement of microbial-recognition receptors can induce production of:

A. Adhesion molecules, cytokines, and other inflammatory mediators
B. Only antibodies
C. Only complement proteins
D. Only collagen
cards.back:
A — Adhesion molecules, cytokines, and other inflammatory mediators

Receptor engagement initiates production of these molecules.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
NOD-like receptors are described as:

A. Membrane receptors exclusively on neutrophils
B. Cytosolic receptors that recognize molecules liberated or altered by cell damage
C. Adhesion molecules on endothelium
D. Complement proteins
cards.back:
B — Cytosolic receptors that recognize molecules liberated or altered by cell damage

NLRs are identified as cytosolic sensors of cellular injury.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Which of the following was identified as a substance sensed during cell damage?

A. Uric acid
B. Hemoglobin only
C. Albumin
D. Collagen only
cards.back:
A — Uric acid

Uric acid is specifically cited among molecules liberated or altered as a consequence of cell damage.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Which damage-associated molecule is released from damaged mitochondria?

A. ATP
B. DNA
C. IL-8
D. C5a
cards.back:
A — ATP

ATP is listed as being released from damaged mitochondria.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Reduced intracellular K⁺ concentration reflects:

A. Increased protein synthesis
B. Loss of ions because of plasma membrane injury
C. Excessive complement activation
D. Increased osmotic pressure
cards.back:
B — Loss of ions because of plasma membrane injury

Robbins directly links reduced intracellular K⁺ to ion loss after plasma membrane injury.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
DNA can function as a danger signal when it is:

A. Confined normally within the nucleus
B. Released into the cytoplasm and not appropriately sequestered in nuclei
C. Bound to histones inside chromatin
D. Replicated normally
cards.back:
B — Released into the cytoplasm and not appropriately sequestered in nuclei

Cytoplasmic DNA is specifically included among damage-associated signals.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Activation of the inflammasome induces production of:

A. TNF only
B. IL-1
C. IgG
D. C3b
cards.back:
B — IL-1

The inflammasome is described as inducing production of the cytokine interleukin-1 (IL-1).

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
IL-1 promotes inflammation principally by:

A. Inhibiting leukocyte recruitment
B. Recruiting leukocytes
C. Blocking endothelial activation
D. Preventing cytokine production
cards.back:
B — Recruiting leukocytes

The text explicitly states that IL-1 recruits leukocytes and thereby induces inflammation.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Gain-of-function mutations affecting some receptors can cause:

A. Autoinflammatory syndromes with spontaneous IL-1 production and inflammation
B. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency exclusively
C. Complement deficiency
D. Hemophilia
cards.back:
A — Autoinflammatory syndromes with spontaneous IL-1 production and inflammation

Gain-of-function mutations in certain receptor genes produce rare autoinflammatory syndromes characterized by spontaneous IL-1 production.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
A treatment described as effective for these receptor-associated autoinflammatory syndromes is:

A. Integrin agonists
B. IL-1 antagonists
C. Histamine agonists
D. Complement inhibitors only
cards.back:
B — IL-1 antagonists

The provided passage specifically states that IL-1 antagonists are effective treatments.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
The inflammasome has been implicated in inflammation caused by:

A. Urate crystals
B. Cholesterol crystals
C. Amyloid deposits
D. All of the above
cards.back:
D — All of the above

The text links the inflammasome to urate crystals in gout, cholesterol crystals in atherosclerosis, and amyloid deposits in Alzheimer disease, as well as lipids in metabolic disease.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Opsonization refers to:

A. Migration of leukocytes into tissues
B. Coating of microbes with antibodies and complement
C. Digestion of microbes within phagolysosomes
D. Activation of fibroblasts
cards.back:
B — Coating of microbes with antibodies and complement

Leukocyte Fc and complement receptors recognize microbes coated with these molecules; the coating process is called opsonization.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Mannose-binding lectin promotes:

A. Only vasodilation
B. Microbial ingestion and complement activation
C. Fibrosis alone
D. Leukocyte apoptosis
cards.back:
B — Microbial ingestion and complement activation

Mannose-binding lectin recognizes microbial sugars and promotes ingestion and complement activation.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Tissue necrosis elicits inflammation:

A. Only when due to infection
B. Only when due to ischemia
C. Regardless of the cause of cell death
D. Only when accompanied by fever
cards.back:
C — Regardless of the cause of cell death

Robbins explicitly states that tissue necrosis causes inflammation irrespective of how the cells died.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Myocardial infarction is described as an example of tissue necrosis due to:

A. Trauma
B. Ischemia
C. Irradiation
D. Chemical toxicity
cards.back:
B — Ischemia

Ischemia means reduced blood flow and is given as the cause of myocardial infarction in this discussion.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Which is an example of a foreign body listed in the chapter?

A. Splinter
B. Albumin
C. Neutrophil
D. Complement
cards.back:
A — Splinter

Splinters, dirt, and sutures are specifically mentioned.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Which endogenous substance is associated with gout?

A. Cholesterol crystals
B. Urate crystals
C. Amyloid
D. Fibrin
cards.back:
B — Urate crystals

Urate crystal deposition is cited as a cause of inflammation in gout.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Immune reactions called hypersensitivity are characterized by:

A. Protection of tissues without injury
B. Damage by the normally protective immune system to the individual's own tissues
C. Selective activation of fibroblasts
D. Complete elimination of antigen
cards.back:
B — Damage by the normally protective immune system to the individual's own tissues

Robbins defines hypersensitivity in this context as immune-mediated tissue injury.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Autoimmune inflammatory reactions are directed against:

A. Environmental substances only
B. Self antigens
C. Microbial toxins only
D. Foreign bodies only
cards.back:
B — Self antigens

The text specifically distinguishes self-antigen reactions causing autoimmune disease from reactions to environmental substances causing allergies.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Why do autoimmune and allergic inflammatory reactions tend to persist?

A. Their stimuli cannot be eliminated
B. They always involve neutrophils
C. They always occur only in blood
D. They are always caused by microorganisms
cards.back:
A — Their stimuli cannot be eliminated

Self antigens and environmental antigens cannot simply be eradicated, producing persistent reactions.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
In autoimmune and allergic inflammation, inflammatory cytokines are produced largely by:

A. T lymphocytes and other immune cells
B. Erythrocytes
C. Fibroblasts only
D. Platelets only
cards.back:
A — T lymphocytes and other immune cells

The passage states that inflammation is induced largely by cytokines produced by T lymphocytes and other immune-system cells.

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front: Describe the role of the inflammasome in inflammation.
cards.back:
The inflammasome is a multiprotein cytosolic complex activated by cellular danger signals; it induces production of IL-1, which recruits leukocytes and promotes inflammation.

Key points:
• Cytosolic multiprotein complex
• Activated by cellular damage signals
• Produces IL-1
• IL-1 recruits leukocytes
• Implicated in gout, metabolic disease, atherosclerosis, Alzheimer disease

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front: What is opsonization?
cards.back:
Opsonization is the coating of microbes with antibodies and complement, facilitating their recognition, ingestion, destruction, and inflammatory responses by leukocytes.

Key points:
• Microbial coating
• Antibodies
• Complement
• Leukocyte receptors
• Enhanced ingestion/destruction

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front: Describe the major sensors involved in recognition of microbes and damaged cells.
cards.back:
Microbial sensors include receptors in the plasma membrane, endosomes, and cytosol, particularly TLRs; damage sensors include cytosolic NLRs that recognize molecules released or altered by cell injury.

Key points:
• Plasma membrane
• Endosomes
• Cytosol
• TLRs
• NLRs

— Recognition of microbes and damaged cells

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT one of the three major components of acute inflammation?

A. Dilation of small vessels
B. Increased microvascular permeability
C. Leukocyte emigration and activation
D. Immediate collagen deposition
cards.back:
D — Immediate collagen deposition

The three major components are vasodilation, increased permeability, and leukocyte emigration/accumulation/activation.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
The primary purpose of vascular reactions in acute inflammation is to:

A. Minimize movement of plasma proteins out of blood
B. Maximize movement of plasma proteins and leukocytes to the site of injury
C. Prevent endothelial activation
D. Initiate fibrosis immediately
cards.back:
B — Maximize movement of plasma proteins and leukocytes to the site of injury

The vascular response is designed to facilitate movement of plasma proteins and leukocytes out of the circulation.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Exudation is:

A. Passage of fluid, proteins, and blood cells from vessels into tissues/body cavities
B. Movement of leukocytes only
C. Movement of red cells only
D. Loss of intracellular fluid
cards.back:
A — Passage of fluid, proteins, and blood cells from vessels into tissues/body cavities

The text defines exudation as escape of fluid, proteins, and blood cells from the vascular system into tissues or body cavities.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
An exudate is characterized by:

A. Low protein concentration and low specific gravity
B. High protein concentration and cellular debris
C. No cellular material
D. Purely osmotic fluid loss
cards.back:
B — High protein concentration and cellular debris

Exudates are extravascular fluids with high protein concentration and cellular debris.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
The presence of an exudate implies:

A. Decreased vascular permeability
B. Increased permeability of small blood vessels
C. Decreased hydrostatic pressure only
D. Decreased blood flow without endothelial change
cards.back:
B — Increased permeability of small blood vessels

Robbins contrasts exudate with transudate and states that exudation implies increased permeability of small vessels.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
A transudate is best described as:

A. Protein-rich inflammatory fluid
B. High-cell fluid caused by endothelial necrosis
C. Low-protein ultrafiltrate produced by osmotic or hydrostatic imbalance without increased vascular permeability
D. Pus
cards.back:
C — Low-protein ultrafiltrate produced by osmotic or hydrostatic imbalance without increased vascular permeability

This is the key distinction between transudate and exudate.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Most of the protein in a transudate is:

A. IgG
B. Albumin
C. Fibrinogen
D. C3b
cards.back:
B — Albumin

Robbins states that most of the low protein content is albumin.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Edema refers to:

A. Only intracellular fluid accumulation
B. Excess fluid in interstitial tissue or serous cavities
C. Only plasma protein accumulation
D. Only pus formation
cards.back:
B — Excess fluid in interstitial tissue or serous cavities

Edema can be caused by either exudate or transudate.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Pus is:

A. A transudate rich in albumin
B. A purulent exudate rich in neutrophils, dead-cell debris, and often microbes
C. A lymphatic fluid
D. A protein-free ultrafiltrate
cards.back:
B — A purulent exudate rich in neutrophils, dead-cell debris, and often microbes

This is the exact description provided.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Vasodilation in acute inflammation is induced notably by:

A. Histamine
B. Collagen
C. IgG
D. C3b only
cards.back:
A — Histamine

Histamine acts on vascular smooth muscle and is a notable mediator of vasodilation.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
The first vascular beds to undergo vasodilation are the:

A. Postcapillary venules
B. Arterioles
C. Lymphatics
D. Large veins
cards.back:
B — Arterioles

Vasodilation first involves arterioles, followed by opening of new capillary beds.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Increased blood flow during acute inflammation causes:

A. Pallor and cooling
B. Heat and redness
C. Cyanosis and pain exclusively
D. Fibrosis
cards.back:
B — Heat and redness

Increased blood flow produces heat and redness/erythema at the inflammatory site.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Vasodilation is generally followed quickly by:

A. Decreased vascular permeability
B. Increased microvascular permeability with protein-rich fluid escape
C. Immediate fibrosis
D. Lymph-node atrophy
cards.back:
B — Increased microvascular permeability with protein-rich fluid escape

This sequence is explicitly described in the vascular changes of acute inflammation.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Loss of fluid from vessels and increased vessel diameter result in:

A. Faster blood flow
B. Slower blood flow and stasis
C. Reduced blood viscosity
D. Leukopenia
cards.back:
B — Slower blood flow and stasis

Fluid loss plus increased vessel diameter slows blood flow, concentrates RBCs, increases viscosity, and produces stasis.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Stasis is characterized by:

A. Rapidly moving platelets
B. Engorgement of small vessels with slowly moving red cells
C. Complete vessel thrombosis
D. Absence of leukocytes from vessel walls
cards.back:
B — Engorgement of small vessels with slowly moving red cells

This is the definition given in the text.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
During stasis, blood leukocytes—principally ______—accumulate along the endothelium.

A. Lymphocytes
B. Neutrophils
C. Eosinophils
D. Basophils
cards.back:
B — Neutrophils

Neutrophils are the principal leukocytes that accumulate along the endothelial surface during stasis.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
Endothelial cells activated by inflammatory mediators:

A. Decrease adhesion molecule expression
B. Express increased levels of adhesion molecules
C. Become impermeable to leukocytes
D. Stop responding to cytokines
cards.back:
B — Express increased levels of adhesion molecules

Endothelial activation increases adhesion molecule expression and promotes leukocyte adhesion and migration.

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front: Define exudate, transudate, edema, and pus.
cards.back:
• Exudate: protein-rich extravascular fluid containing cellular debris due to increased vascular permeability. • Transudate: low-protein ultrafiltrate caused by hydrostatic/osmotic imbalance without increased permeability. • Edema: excess fluid in interstitial tissue or serous cavities. • Pus: purulent exudate rich in neutrophils, dead-cell debris, and often microbes.

Key points:
• Protein concentration
• Cellular content
• Mechanism
• Exudate vs transudate
• Pus as inflammatory exudate

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front: Describe the sequence of vascular changes in acute inflammation.
cards.back:
Vasodilation begins in arterioles, opens new capillary beds and increases blood flow; increased permeability then causes protein-rich fluid leakage, followed by fluid loss, hemoconcentration, slowed flow, and stasis.

Key points:
• Arteriolar vasodilation
• Increased blood flow
• Capillary-bed opening
• Increased permeability
• Protein-rich leakage
• Stasis

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front: What are the three major components of acute inflammation?
cards.back:
Small-vessel dilation with increased blood flow; increased microvascular permeability; leukocyte emigration, accumulation, and activation at the inflammatory focus.

Key points:
• Vasodilation
• Permeability
• Leukocyte recruitment
• Leukocyte activation
• Elimination of offending agent

— Acute inflammation and reactions of blood vessels

cards.front:
The most common mechanism of vascular leakage is:

A. Endothelial necrosis
B. Contraction of endothelial cells causing interendothelial gaps
C. Direct vessel thrombosis
D. Fibroblast contraction
cards.back:
B — Contraction of endothelial cells causing interendothelial gaps

Robbins identifies endothelial contraction with gap formation as the most common mechanism.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
The immediate transient response of vascular leakage is usually:

A. Delayed for 2–12 hours
B. Present for days
C. Rapid and short-lived, approximately 15–30 minutes
D. Permanent
cards.back:
C — Rapid and short-lived, approximately 15–30 minutes

The immediate transient response occurs rapidly after mediator exposure and usually lasts 15–30 minutes.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Which mediators are specifically listed as causing endothelial contraction and interendothelial gap formation?

A. Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotrienes
B. C3b, IgG, and collagen
C. TNF only
D. IL-8 only
cards.back:
A — Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotrienes

These are specifically named in the text.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Delayed prolonged vascular leakage may begin:

A. Immediately and last only 1 minute
B. After 2–12 hours
C. After several weeks
D. Only after leukocyte apoptosis
cards.back:
B — After 2–12 hours

Delayed prolonged leakage begins after 2–12 hours and can persist for hours or days.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Which is the classic example of delayed prolonged vascular leakage in the provided text?

A. Myocardial infarction
B. Sunburn
C. Arthritis
D. Glomerulonephritis
cards.back:
B — Sunburn

Sunburn is described as a classic example of late-appearing vascular leakage.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Mild burns can produce delayed prolonged leakage due to:

A. Only complement activation
B. Endothelial contraction or mild endothelial damage
C. Fibroblast proliferation only
D. Platelet destruction
cards.back:
B — Endothelial contraction or mild endothelial damage

Both mechanisms are described for delayed leakage after mild injuries.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Direct endothelial injury is encountered in severe physical injury such as:

A. Thermal burns
B. Mild exercise
C. Hyperglycemia alone
D. Normal aging
cards.back:
A — Thermal burns

Severe thermal burns are explicitly cited as producing direct endothelial damage.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Endothelial injury can also be caused by:

A. Microbes and microbial toxins
B. Albumin
C. Fibronectin alone
D. RBCs
cards.back:
A — Microbes and microbial toxins

Both microbes and microbial toxins can directly damage endothelial cells.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Neutrophils adhering to endothelium can:

A. Prevent vascular leakage
B. Injure endothelial cells and amplify inflammation
C. Always terminate inflammation
D. Inhibit adhesion molecule expression
cards.back:
B — Injure endothelial cells and amplify inflammation

Adherent neutrophils may themselves damage endothelial cells, amplifying vascular leakage and inflammation.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
In most instances, leakage caused by direct endothelial injury:

A. Begins immediately and can be sustained for several hours
B. Begins only after several days
C. Is always transient for less than 30 seconds
D. Occurs only after fibrosis
cards.back:
A — Begins immediately and can be sustained for several hours

Leakage begins immediately and persists until vessels thrombose or are repaired.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
In severe burns, vascular leakage may cause:

A. Life-threatening fluid loss
B. Only mild erythema
C. Immediate fibrosis without edema
D. Leukopenia without fluid change
cards.back:
A — Life-threatening fluid loss

Severe burns can produce devastating vascular leakage and fluid loss.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Lymphatics in acute inflammation normally:

A. Decrease flow
B. Increase flow and help drain edema fluid
C. Stop functioning
D. Become completely impermeable
cards.back:
B — Increase flow and help drain edema fluid

Increased lymphatic flow assists drainage of the edema generated by increased vascular permeability.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
During inflammation, lymph may contain all of the following EXCEPT:

A. Leukocytes
B. Cell debris
C. Microbes
D. Only albumin with no cells
cards.back:
D — Only albumin with no cells

Leukocytes, cellular debris, and microbes can all enter lymph during inflammation.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Lymphatic vessels during inflammation:

A. Do not proliferate
B. May proliferate to handle the increased load
C. Always thrombose
D. Become permanently atrophic
cards.back:
B — May proliferate to handle the increased load

Lymphatics can proliferate during inflammatory reactions to accommodate increased drainage.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Inflammation of lymphatic vessels is termed:

A. Lymphadenitis
B. Lymphangitis
C. Lymphoma
D. Lymphocytosis
cards.back:
B — Lymphangitis

Inflammation of lymphatic channels is called lymphangitis.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Inflammation of draining lymph nodes is termed:

A. Lymphangitis
B. Lymphadenitis
C. Lymphostasis
D. Lymphocytopenia
cards.back:
B — Lymphadenitis

The draining lymph nodes may become inflamed, producing lymphadenitis.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Reactive lymphadenitis causes lymph-node enlargement primarily because of:

A. Follicular hyperplasia and increased lymphocytes/macrophages
B. Fat necrosis only
C. Decreased lymphocyte number
D. Fibroblast depletion
cards.back:
A — Follicular hyperplasia and increased lymphocytes/macrophages

Hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and increased lymphocytes and macrophages enlarge the nodes.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Red streaks extending from a skin wound represent:

A. Venous thrombosis
B. Inflamed lymphatic channels
C. Arterial vasospasm
D. Fibrosis
cards.back:
B — Inflamed lymphatic channels

The text identifies these red streaks as a telltale sign of bacterial infection caused by lymphangitis.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Painful enlargement of draining lymph nodes in this setting suggests:

A. Lymphadenitis
B. Lymphoma
C. Thrombophlebitis
D. Edema only
cards.back:
A — Lymphadenitis

Painful enlarged draining nodes indicate inflammation of those nodes.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
According to Figure 3.2, normal hydrostatic pressure is approximately:

A. 12 mm Hg at arterial and 32 mm Hg at venous ends
B. 32 mm Hg at the arterial end and 12 mm Hg at the venous end
C. 25 mm Hg at both ends
D. 40 mm Hg at the arterial end and 25 mm Hg at the venous end
cards.back:
B — 32 mm Hg at the arterial end and 12 mm Hg at the venous end

Figure 3.2 gives hydrostatic pressure as about 32 mm Hg arterial and 12 mm Hg venous.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
The mean colloid osmotic pressure of tissues in Figure 3.2 is approximately:

A. 5 mm Hg
B. 12 mm Hg
C. 25 mm Hg
D. 32 mm Hg
cards.back:
C — 25 mm Hg

The figure states a mean tissue colloid osmotic pressure of approximately 25 mm Hg.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
A transudate forms primarily because of:

A. Increased interendothelial gaps
B. Increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased osmotic pressure
C. Endothelial necrosis only
D. Leukocyte adhesion
cards.back:
B — Increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased osmotic pressure

Figure 3.2 contrasts the hydrostatic/osmotic mechanism of transudate with permeability-mediated exudate.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
An exudate forms in inflammation because:

A. Vascular permeability increases through increased interendothelial spaces
B. Plasma colloid osmotic pressure always rises
C. Hydrostatic pressure falls
D. Vascular endothelium becomes completely impermeable
cards.back:
A — Vascular permeability increases through increased interendothelial spaces

This is the mechanism shown in Figure 3.2B.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Which pairing is correctly matched?

A. Retraction/contraction of endothelial cells — histamine and other mediators
B. Endothelial injury — only chemokines
C. Retraction — hours to days
D. Endothelial injury — always brief and transient
cards.back:
A — Retraction/contraction of endothelial cells — histamine and other mediators

Figure 3.3 identifies histamine/other mediators with rapid short-lived endothelial retraction, while endothelial injury may last hours to days.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
Endothelial injury caused by thermal burns or microbial toxins may produce leakage that is:

A. Rapid and potentially long-lived
B. Delayed for weeks only
C. Always limited to 15 minutes
D. Absent initially
cards.back:
A — Rapid and potentially long-lived

Figure 3.3 specifically describes endothelial injury as rapid and potentially prolonged for hours to days.

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front: Describe the mechanisms of increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation covered so far.
cards.back:
The most common mechanism is endothelial contraction/retraction causing interendothelial gaps; delayed prolonged leakage may follow some mild injuries, while direct endothelial injury or leukocyte-mediated endothelial damage can cause rapid and sustained leakage.

Key points:
• Endothelial contraction
• Interendothelial gaps
• Immediate transient response
• Delayed prolonged leakage
• Direct endothelial injury
• Neutrophil-mediated endothelial injury

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front: Describe the lymphatic response in acute inflammation.
cards.back:
Lymphatic flow increases to drain edema; leukocytes, debris, and microbes may enter lymph; lymphatics may proliferate and become inflamed (lymphangitis), while draining nodes may enlarge due to reactive lymphadenitis.

Key points:
• Increased lymph flow
• Edema drainage
• Leukocytes/debris/microbes in lymph
• Lymphatic proliferation
• Lymphangitis
• Lymphadenitis

— Increased vascular permeability and lymphatic responses

cards.front:
The first phase of leukocyte recruitment occurs:

A. In the tissue
B. In the lumen and includes margination, rolling, and adhesion
C. In lymph nodes
D. In bone marrow
cards.back:
B — In the lumen and includes margination, rolling, and adhesion

Robbins divides leukocyte recruitment into sequential phases beginning in the vascular lumen.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Normal vascular endothelium:

A. Actively binds circulating leukocytes
B. Does not normally bind circulating cells or permit their passage
C. Expresses maximal E-selectin continuously
D. Permits unrestricted leukocyte migration
cards.back:
B — Does not normally bind circulating cells or permit their passage

In inflammation, endothelial activation changes this property and permits leukocyte recruitment.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Margination results from:

A. Increased RBC velocity
B. Redistribution of leukocytes toward the endothelial surface during slowed blood flow
C. Leukocyte apoptosis
D. Increased plasma oncotic pressure
cards.back:
B — Redistribution of leukocytes toward the endothelial surface during slowed blood flow

Stasis pushes more leukocytes toward the vessel wall; this redistribution is called margination.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Leukocyte margination occurs particularly because:

A. Red cells move into the vessel wall
B. Red cells occupy a central axial column, displacing leukocytes toward the wall
C. Leukocytes become heavier than RBCs
D. Plasma proteins bind leukocytes
cards.back:
B — Red cells occupy a central axial column, displacing leukocytes toward the wall

This is the physical basis described in flowing venular blood.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which molecules mediate the initial rolling interactions?

A. Integrins
B. Selectins
C. CD31 alone
D. PECAM-independent collagen
cards.back:
B — Selectins

Selectins mediate the initial rolling phase, whereas integrins mediate firm adhesion.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Selectin-mediated leukocyte-endothelial interactions are typically:

A. High-affinity and irreversible
B. Low-affinity with a fast off-rate
C. Mediated by IgG
D. Independent of blood flow
cards.back:
B — Low-affinity with a fast off-rate

These transient interactions allow leukocytes to repeatedly bind and detach, producing rolling.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Firm leukocyte adhesion is mediated principally by:

A. Selectins
B. Integrins
C. Histamine
D. Complement
cards.back:
B — Integrins

Firm adhesion is mediated by heterodimeric leukocyte-surface integrins.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
TNF and IL-1 induce endothelial expression mainly of:

A. VCAM-1 and ICAM-1
B. IgG and C3b
C. PECAM alone
D. Histamine receptors only
cards.back:
A — VCAM-1 and ICAM-1

TNF/IL-1 induce integrin ligands, principally VCAM-1 and ICAM-1.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
VCAM-1 is the ligand for:

A. LFA-1
B. MAC-1
C. VLA-4
D. CD31
cards.back:
C — VLA-4

VCAM-1 is described as the ligand for the β1 integrin VLA-4.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
ICAM-1 is the ligand for:

A. VLA-4 only
B. β2 integrins LFA-1 and MAC-1
C. L-selectin
D. P-selectin
cards.back:
B — β2 integrins LFA-1 and MAC-1

Robbins specifically pairs ICAM-1 with LFA-1 and MAC-1.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Leukocyte integrins are normally expressed in a:

A. High-affinity state
B. Low-affinity state
C. Irreversibly inactive state
D. Cytoplasmic-only state
cards.back:
B — Low-affinity state

Chemokines then activate these integrins, increasing their affinity.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Chemokines that activate rolling leukocytes are displayed on the endothelial surface by binding to:

A. Collagen
B. Proteoglycans
C. Albumin
D. Fibroblasts
cards.back:
B — Proteoglycans

Endothelial proteoglycans bind chemokines and present them at high concentrations on the endothelial surface.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Chemokine-mediated activation converts VLA-4 and LFA-1 to:

A. Low-affinity forms
B. High-affinity forms
C. Soluble proteins
D. Selectins
cards.back:
B — High-affinity forms

Chemokines increase integrin affinity, allowing firm adhesion.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Firm adhesion results from the combination of:

A. Reduced integrin affinity + reduced ligand expression
B. Cytokine-induced endothelial ligand expression + increased leukocyte integrin affinity
C. Selectin loss + complement activation
D. Increased RBC velocity + endothelial injury
cards.back:
B — Cytokine-induced endothelial ligand expression + increased leukocyte integrin affinity

Both changes are required for stable integrin-mediated adhesion.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Following firm adhesion, leukocytes:

A. Continue rolling indefinitely
B. Stop rolling, reorganize their cytoskeleton, and spread on the endothelium
C. Immediately undergo apoptosis
D. Return to the bloodstream
cards.back:
B — Stop rolling, reorganize their cytoskeleton, and spread on the endothelium

These changes occur after firm integrin-mediated adhesion.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which selectin is expressed on leukocytes?

A. E-selectin
B. P-selectin
C. L-selectin
D. ICAM-1
cards.back:
C — L-selectin

L-selectin is the leukocyte selectin; E-selectin is endothelial and P-selectin is on platelets/endothelium.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
E-selectin is expressed on:

A. Leukocytes only
B. Activated endothelium
C. Platelets only
D. RBCs
cards.back:
B — Activated endothelium

E-selectin is an endothelial selectin induced during inflammation.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
P-selectin is found on:

A. Platelets and endothelium
B. Neutrophils only
C. T cells only
D. Macrophages only
cards.back:
A — Platelets and endothelium

This is the specific distribution given for P-selectin.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Selectin ligands are:

A. Sialylated oligosaccharides on mucin-like glycoproteins
B. Integrins on platelets
C. Immunoglobulins
D. Complement fragments
cards.back:
A — Sialylated oligosaccharides on mucin-like glycoproteins

Robbins describes selectin ligands in these terms.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
TNF and IL-1 induce endothelial cells to begin expressing E-selectin and L-selectin ligands within approximately:

A. 1–2 minutes
B. 1–2 hours
C. 24–48 hours
D. 1 week
cards.back:
B — 1–2 hours

The text gives the timing as within 1–2 hours.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Histamine and thrombin promote redistribution of P-selectin from:

A. Nuclei to lysosomes
B. Weibel-Palade bodies to the cell surface
C. Mitochondria to cytosol
D. Golgi to nucleus
cards.back:
B — Weibel-Palade bodies to the cell surface

P-selectin is stored in endothelial granules called Weibel-Palade bodies and redistributed to the cell surface.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Leukocyte L-selectin is located at the:

A. Nucleus
B. Tips of microvilli
C. Golgi apparatus
D. Phagosome
cards.back:
B — Tips of microvilli

This exact location is stated in the text.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
LFA-1 is designated:

A. CD62L
B. CD11a/CD18
C. CD11b/CD18
D. CD49a/CD29
cards.back:
B — CD11a/CD18

Table 3.3 identifies LFA-1 as CD11a/CD18.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
MAC-1 is:

A. CD11a/CD18
B. CD11b/CD18
C. CD49a/CD29
D. CD49d/CD29
cards.back:
B — CD11b/CD18

Table 3.3 identifies MAC-1 as CD11b/CD18.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
VLA-4 is:

A. CD49a/CD29
B. CD11b/CD18
C. CD62E
D. CD31
cards.back:
A — CD49a/CD29

Table 3.3 lists VLA-4 as CD49a/CD29.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
α4β7 is identified in Table 3.3 as:

A. CD49d/CD29
B. CD11a/CD18
C. CD62P
D. CD54
cards.back:
A — CD49d/CD29

The table identifies α4β7 as CD49d/CD29 and associates it with gut homing.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
CD31/PECAM-1 is involved primarily in:

A. Rolling
B. Firm adhesion
C. Transmigration
D. Chemotaxis
cards.back:
C — Transmigration

CD31 is located at endothelial junctions and is a key molecule in leukocyte transmigration.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Leukocyte migration through intact endothelium is called:

A. Margination
B. Rolling
C. Transmigration/diapedesis
D. Opsonization
cards.back:
C — Transmigration/diapedesis

The text uses both terms for passage through intact endothelium.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Transmigration occurs mainly through:

A. Arterioles
B. Capillaries
C. Postcapillary venules
D. Large veins
cards.back:
C — Postcapillary venules

Postcapillary venules are the principal site of leukocyte transmigration.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
After crossing the endothelium, leukocytes penetrate the basement membrane probably by secreting:

A. Elastase only
B. Collagenases
C. Histamine
D. Complement
cards.back:
B — Collagenases

The text says they probably pierce the basement membrane by secreting collagenases.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
After leukocytes pass through, the basement membranes:

A. Remain permanently discontinuous
B. Become continuous again
C. Are replaced by thrombus
D. Undergo calcification
cards.back:
B — Become continuous again

Robbins specifically notes restoration of basement-membrane continuity.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Chemotaxis is defined as:

A. Random movement of leukocytes
B. Locomotion along a chemical gradient
C. Firm adhesion to endothelial cells
D. Migration through lymphatics
cards.back:
B — Locomotion along a chemical gradient

This is the definition given by Robbins.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which is an exogenous chemoattractant?

A. IL-8
B. C5a
C. Bacterial peptides containing N-formylmethionine
D. LTB4
cards.back:
C — Bacterial peptides containing N-formylmethionine

Bacterial products, including N-formylmethionine-containing peptides, are major exogenous chemoattractants.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which of the following is an endogenous chemoattractant?

A. N-formylmethionine bacterial peptide
B. IL-8
C. Bacterial lipid only
D. Splinter
cards.back:
B — IL-8

IL-8 is given as an example of a chemokine acting as an endogenous chemoattractant.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
The three principal categories of endogenous chemoattractants listed are:

A. Cytokines, complement components, and AA metabolites
B. IgG, platelets, and RBCs
C. Histamine, albumin, and collagen
D. Fibroblasts, mast cells, and platelets
cards.back:
A — Cytokines, complement components, and AA metabolites

The text specifically lists chemokines such as IL-8, C5a, and LTB4.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
The complement component specifically identified as chemotactic is:

A. C1q
B. C3b
C. C5a
D. C9
cards.back:
C — C5a

C5a is the complement component specifically listed as an endogenous chemoattractant.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
The major arachidonic-acid metabolite identified as a chemoattractant is:

A. PGE₂
B. TXA₂
C. LTB4
D. PGI₂
cards.back:
C — LTB4

Leukotriene B4 is the principal AA metabolite named.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Chemotactic agents bind leukocytes through:

A. Nuclear receptors only
B. Seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptors
C. Integrin ligands only
D. Toll-like receptors exclusively
cards.back:
B — Seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptors

All these chemotactic agents are described as binding specific seven-transmembrane GPCRs.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Chemotactic signaling induces:

A. Actin polymerization at the trailing edge
B. Actin polymerization at the leading edge and myosin localization at the back
C. Destruction of the cytoskeleton
D. Loss of cell polarity
cards.back:
B — Actin polymerization at the leading edge and myosin localization at the back

This cytoskeletal reorganization produces directional locomotion.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
The extension at the leading edge involved in leukocyte migration is:

A. Microvillus only
B. Filopodium
C. Cilium
D. Axoneme
cards.back:
B — Filopodium

The text describes leading-edge filopodia that pull the trailing portion of the cell forward. Timing and composition of the inflammatory infiltrate

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
In most forms of acute inflammation, neutrophils predominate during:

A. 1–2 hours only
B. 6–24 hours
C. 24–48 hours only
D. Several weeks
cards.back:
B — 6–24 hours

Neutrophils predominate during the first 6–24 hours in most acute inflammatory reactions.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Monocytes generally replace neutrophils during:

A. 0–6 hours
B. 6–12 hours
C. 24–48 hours
D. 5–7 days
cards.back:
C — 24–48 hours

The typical sequence is neutrophils first, followed by monocytes in 24–48 hours.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which is NOT given as a reason for early neutrophil predominance?

A. Neutrophils are more numerous
B. They respond more rapidly to chemokines
C. They may attach more firmly to rapidly induced P- and E-selectins
D. They survive for years in tissues
cards.back:
D — They survive for years in tissues

Neutrophils are actually short-lived in extravascular tissues.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Most extravascular neutrophils undergo apoptosis within:

A. Hours only
B. A few days
C. Several months
D. Years
cards.back:
B — A few days

Robbins specifically describes neutrophils as short-lived after entering tissues.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Monocytes can become dominant in prolonged inflammation because they:

A. Are rapidly destroyed
B. Survive longer and may proliferate in tissues
C. Cannot migrate into tissues
D. Lack phagocytic activity
cards.back:
B — Survive longer and may proliferate in tissues

Their longer survival and ability to proliferate favor their dominance in prolonged reactions.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Pseudomonas infection may characteristically produce an infiltrate dominated by:

A. Continuously recruited neutrophils for several days
B. Plasma cells only
C. Eosinophils only
D. Fibroblasts
cards.back:
A — Continuously recruited neutrophils for several days

Pseudomonas is given as an exception to the usual neutrophil-to-monocyte pattern.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
In some viral infections, the first cells to arrive may be:

A. Neutrophils exclusively
B. Lymphocytes
C. Eosinophils
D. Fibroblasts
cards.back:
B — Lymphocytes

Viral infections are specifically mentioned as an exception where lymphocytes may arrive first.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Helminthic infections and allergic reactions may be dominated by:

A. Neutrophils
B. Eosinophils
C. Monocytes
D. Platelets
cards.back:
B — Eosinophils

Eosinophils are the characteristic predominant cell type mentioned for helminthic and allergic reactions.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Some hypersensitivity reactions are dominated by:

A. Activated lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells
B. Neutrophils only
C. Eosinophils only
D. RBCs and platelets
cards.back:
A — Activated lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells

The text links this infiltrate to the immune response.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Blocking leukocyte integrins may:

A. Reduce inflammation but increase microbial defense
B. Control inflammation while compromising host defense against microbes
C. Always increase neutrophilia
D. Have no effect on inflammatory disease
cards.back:
B — Control inflammation while compromising host defense against microbes

The therapeutic benefit comes with impaired physiologic inflammatory defense against microbes.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Genetic deficiencies of leukocyte adhesion molecules result in:

A. Increased susceptibility to bacterial infections
B. Decreased susceptibility to infection
C. Polycythemia
D. Fibrosis only
cards.back:
A — Increased susceptibility to bacterial infections

Leukocyte adhesion deficiencies illustrate the importance of adhesion molecules in host inflammatory defense.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which sequence is correct?

A. Firm adhesion → rolling → chemotaxis → margination
B. Rolling → integrin activation → stable adhesion → transmigration → chemotaxis
C. Chemotaxis → rolling → margination → adhesion
D. Transmigration → rolling → opsonization → margination
cards.back:
B — Rolling → integrin activation → stable adhesion → transmigration → chemotaxis

Figure 3.4 illustrates this multistep recruitment sequence.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which molecule is most specifically associated with rolling?

A. Integrin
B. Selectin
C. CD31
D. LTB4
cards.back:
B — Selectin

Figure 3.4 explicitly assigns selectins to rolling.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which molecule is most specifically associated with firm adhesion?

A. Selectin
B. Integrin
C. CD31
D. Histamine
cards.back:
B — Integrin

Integrins mediate firm adhesion after activation by chemokines.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
Which molecule is most specifically associated with transmigration?

A. CD31/PECAM-1
B. E-selectin
C. P-selectin
D. VCAM-1
cards.back:
A — CD31/PECAM-1

CD31/PECAM-1 is the molecule highlighted for transmigration.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
The predominant role of chemokines in leukocyte recruitment is:

A. Causing firm adhesion directly without integrin activation
B. Activating leukocytes to increase integrin avidity and promoting directional migration
C. Forming the basement membrane
D. Destroying microbes directly
cards.back:
B — Activating leukocytes to increase integrin avidity and promoting directional migration

Figure 3.4 and the associated text assign chemokines these functions.

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front: Describe leukocyte recruitment as a multistep process.
cards.back:
Leukocyte recruitment involves margination, selectin-mediated rolling, chemokine- mediated integrin activation, integrin-mediated firm adhesion, transmigration through postcapillary venules, basement-membrane penetration, and chemotactic migration through tissues.

Key points:
• Margination
• Rolling
• Integrin activation
• Firm adhesion
• Transmigration/diapedesis
• Chemotaxis

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front: Describe the roles of selectins, integrins, chemokines, and PECAM-1 in leukocyte recruitment.
cards.back:
Selectins mediate rolling; chemokines activate leukocyte integrins; integrins mediate firm adhesion; PECAM-1/CD31 mediates transmigration.

Key points:
• Selectins → rolling
• Chemokines → integrin activation
• Integrins → firm adhesion
• CD31 → transmigration

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front: Describe chemotaxis.
cards.back:
Chemotaxis is leukocyte locomotion along a chemical gradient toward the inflammatory stimulus. It is driven by exogenous bacterial products and endogenous chemokines, C5a, and LTB4 acting through GPCRs and inducing cytoskeletal reorganization.

Key points:
• Chemical gradient
• Exogenous and endogenous chemoattractants
• N-formylmethionine
• IL-8/C5a/LTB4
• GPCRs
• Actin/myosin rearrangement

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front: Describe the typical time course and exceptions of leukocyte infiltration in acute inflammation.
cards.back:
Neutrophils usually predominate during 6–24 hours, followed by monocytes at 24–48 hours. Exceptions include prolonged neutrophilia in Pseudomonas infection, early lymphocytes in some viral infections, lymphocytes/macrophages/plasma cells in some hypersensitivity reactions, and eosinophils in helminthic/allergic reactions.

Key points:
• Neutrophils: 6–24 h
• Monocytes: 24–48 h
• Pseudomonas → prolonged neutrophils
• Viral → lymphocytes may arrive first
• Hypersensitivity → lymphocytes/macrophages/plasma cells
• Helminths/allergy → eosinophils

— Leukocyte recruitment, adhesion, migration, and chemotaxis

cards.front:
The two major phagocytes are:

A. Eosinophils and plasma cells
B. Neutrophils and macrophages
C. B cells and T cells
D. Mast cells and platelets
cards.back:
B — Neutrophils and macrophages

These are identified as the two major phagocytic cell types.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Recognition of microbes or dead cells induces a collection of leukocyte responses called:

A. Transmigration
B. Leukocyte activation
C. Opsonization
D. Chemotaxis
cards.back:
B — Leukocyte activation

The collective responses induced by recognition are termed leukocyte activation.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Leukocyte activation produces an increase in:

A. Cytosolic Ca²⁺
B. Cytosolic Na⁺ only
C. Extracellular K⁺ only
D. Nuclear calcium exclusively
cards.back:
A — Cytosolic Ca²⁺

The signaling pathways of activation increase cytosolic Ca²⁺.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Enzymes activated during leukocyte activation include:

A. Protein kinase C and phospholipase A₂
B. DNA polymerase and topoisomerase
C. Renin and pepsin
D. Amylase and lipase only
cards.back:
A — Protein kinase C and phospholipase A₂

Both enzymes are specifically mentioned.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
The two most important leukocyte responses for destruction of microbes are:

A. Chemotaxis and rolling
B. Phagocytosis and intracellular killing
C. Fibrosis and angiogenesis
D. Adhesion and margination
cards.back:
B — Phagocytosis and intracellular killing

These are specifically identified as the principal destructive functions.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Phagocytosis consists of how many sequential major steps in the provided text?

A. Two
B. Three
C. Four
D. Five
cards.back:
B — Three

The three steps are recognition/attachment, engulfment with phagosome formation, and killing/degradation.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
The first step of phagocytosis is:

A. Killing
B. Recognition and attachment
C. Phagolysosome formation
D. Exocytosis
cards.back:
B — Recognition and attachment

Recognition and attachment precede engulfment and intracellular killing.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Engulfment leads to formation of a:

A. Lysosome directly
B. Phagocytic vacuole/phagosome
C. Nucleus
D. Granuloma
cards.back:
B — Phagocytic vacuole/phagosome

Cytoplasmic extensions surround the particle and the membrane pinches off to form a phagosome.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
After phagosome formation, the phagosome fuses with:

A. Mitochondria
B. A lysosomal granule
C. Golgi apparatus
D. Nucleus
cards.back:
B — A lysosomal granule

Fusion allows lysosomal contents to enter the phagosome and participate in killing/degradation.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Which receptors can mediate microbial binding and ingestion?

A. Mannose receptors, scavenger receptors, and opsonin receptors
B. Only selectins
C. Only TLRs
D. Only CD31
cards.back:
A — Mannose receptors, scavenger receptors, and opsonin receptors

These receptor groups are specifically listed in the phagocytosis section.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
The macrophage mannose receptor is a:

A. Kinase
B. Lectin
C. Cytokine
D. Integrin
cards.back:
B — Lectin

It is described as a lectin that binds terminal mannose and fucose residues.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
The mannose receptor binds terminal:

A. Sialic acid only
B. Mannose and fucose
C. Galactose only
D. Glucose only
cards.back:
B — Mannose and fucose

These terminal sugars are recognized on microbial glycoproteins/glycolipids.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Mammalian glycoproteins and glycolipids commonly contain terminal:

A. Mannose and fucose exclusively
B. Sialic acid or N-acetylgalactosamine
C. N-formylmethionine
D. C3b
cards.back:
B — Sialic acid or N-acetylgalactosamine

This distinction allows the mannose receptor to preferentially recognize microbes rather than host cells.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
The macrophage mannose receptor therefore preferentially recognizes:

A. Host cells
B. Microbes
C. RBCs
D. Fibroblasts
cards.back:
B — Microbes

The differing terminal carbohydrate patterns allow discrimination of microbial from mammalian cells.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Scavenger receptors were originally defined based on their ability to mediate uptake of:

A. Native HDL
B. Oxidized or acetylated LDL
C. IgG
D. C5a
cards.back:
B — Oxidized or acetylated LDL

Scavenger receptors were originally defined by binding and mediating endocytosis of modified LDL particles that do not interact with the conventional LDL receptor.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Macrophage scavenger receptors:

A. Bind only modified LDL
B. Bind various microbes in addition to modified LDL
C. Bind only antibodies
D. Function only in endothelial cells
cards.back:
B — Bind various microbes in addition to modified LDL

Robbins specifically expands their role beyond modified LDL uptake.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Which integrin is specifically mentioned as capable of binding microbes for phagocytosis?

A. VLA-4
B. MAC-1
C. LFA-1 only
D. α4β7 only
cards.back:
B — MAC-1

MAC-1 (CD11b/CD18) is specifically mentioned.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Phagocytosis is greatly enhanced when microbes are:

A. Depleted of proteins
B. Coated with opsonins recognized by high-affinity phagocyte receptors
C. Converted into transudates
D. Bound to erythrocytes
cards.back:
B — Coated with opsonins recognized by high-affinity phagocyte receptors

Opsonization greatly enhances phagocytic efficiency.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Which is a major opsonin listed in the text?

A. IgG
B. IgM only
C. IL-1
D. LTB4
cards.back:
A — IgG

Major opsonins include IgG antibodies, C3b, mannose-binding lectin, and collectins.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Which complement product is listed as a major opsonin?

A. C5a
B. C3b
C. C1q only
D. C9
cards.back:
B — C3b

The provided text specifies the C3b breakdown product of complement among the major opsonins.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Which pair represents plasma lectins that function as major opsonins?

A. Histamine and serotonin
B. Mannose-binding lectin and collectins
C. TNF and IL-1
D. LTB4 and C5a
cards.back:
B — Mannose-binding lectin and collectins

Both are listed among the major opsonins.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
After binding to phagocyte receptors, cytoplasmic extensions:

A. Move away from the particle
B. Flow around the particle and enclose it
C. Release histamine
D. Form a granuloma
cards.back:
B — Flow around the particle and enclose it

This produces the intracellular phagosome.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Which statement about phagocytosis is correct?

A. It is independent of actin polymerization
B. It depends on polymerization of actin filaments
C. It occurs without receptor signaling
D. It requires fibrosis first
cards.back:
B — It depends on polymerization of actin filaments

Phagocytosis integrates receptor-generated signals leading to membrane remodeling and cytoskeletal change and depends on actin polymerization.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Figure 3.6 illustrates the inflammatory response in:

A. Liver after viral hepatitis
B. Myocardium after ischemic necrosis/infarction
C. Skin after allergy
D. Lung after tuberculosis
cards.back:
B — Myocardium after ischemic necrosis/infarction

The figure compares early neutrophilic and later mononuclear infiltrates in infarcted myocardium.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
In Figure 3.6, the later inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly:

A. Neutrophilic
B. Mononuclear
C. Eosinophilic
D. Plasma-cell-only
cards.back:
B — Mononuclear

The later photomicrograph demonstrates a mononuclear infiltrate.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
Figure 3.6 notes that edema is shown for simplicity as:

A. Always chronic
B. An acute transient response, although delayed secondary waves may occur
C. Absent in inflammation
D. Completely independent of neutrophils
cards.back:
B — An acute transient response, although delayed secondary waves may occur

The caption explicitly warns that secondary waves of delayed edema and neutrophil infiltration can occur.

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front: Enumerate the steps of phagocytosis.
