cards.back:
Recognition and attachment; engulfment with phagosome formation; killing of the microbe and degradation of ingested material.

Key points:
• Recognition
• Attachment
• Engulfment
• Phagosome
• Killing
• Degradation

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front: List the major phagocytic receptors described.
cards.back:
Mannose receptors, scavenger receptors, receptors for opsonins, and macrophage integrins such as MAC-1.

Key points:
• Mannose receptor
• Scavenger receptors
• Opsonin receptors
• MAC-1
• Microbial recognition/ingestion

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front: List the major opsonins mentioned.
cards.back:
IgG antibodies, C3b, mannose-binding lectin, and collectins.

Key points:
• IgG
• C3b
• Mannose-binding lectin
• Collectins
• High-affinity receptors on phagocytes

— Phagocytosis and clearance of the offending agent

cards.front:
A patient has protein-rich fluid in an inflamed tissue. Which finding most strongly identifies this as an exudate rather than a transudate?

A. Low specific gravity
B. Low protein concentration
C. Increased vascular permeability
D. Hydrostatic imbalance without endothelial change
cards.back:
C — Increased vascular permeability

Exudates result from increased vascular permeability; transudates arise from hydrostatic/osmotic imbalance without increased permeability.

cards.front:
Which pairing is incorrect?

A. Selectins — rolling
B. Integrins — firm adhesion
C. CD31 — transmigration
D. Chemokines — direct phagosome formation
cards.back:
D — Chemokines — direct phagosome formation

Chemokines activate integrins and promote migration; they do not form phagosomes.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
A patient has defective expression of VCAM-1. Which leukocyte molecule would be most directly affected in firm adhesion?

A. L-selectin
B. VLA-4
C. CD31
D. P-selectin
cards.back:
B — VLA-4

VCAM-1 is the ligand for VLA-4.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
A patient has impaired ICAM-1 binding. Which integrins are primarily affected?

A. VLA-4 only
B. LFA-1 and MAC-1
C. α4β7 only
D. L-selectin
cards.back:
B — LFA-1 and MAC-1

ICAM-1 is the endothelial ligand for these β2 integrins.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which leukocyte-recruitment event requires chemokine-induced conversion of integrins from low- to high-affinity states?

A. Margination
B. Rolling
C. Firm adhesion
D. Basement-membrane degradation
cards.back:
C — Firm adhesion

Chemokines increase integrin affinity, allowing stable adhesion to endothelial integrin ligands.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which of the following is the best endogenous chemoattractant among the options?

A. N-formylmethionine
B. C5a
C. Splinter
D. Modified LDL
cards.back:
B — C5a

C5a is specifically listed among endogenous chemoattractants; N-formylmethionine is bacterial/exogenous.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which leukocyte predominates during the first 6–24 hours of most acute inflammatory reactions?

A. Monocyte
B. Neutrophil
C. Lymphocyte
D. Eosinophil
cards.back:
B — Neutrophil

This is the typical timing described in Robbins.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which cell becomes dominant in prolonged inflammatory reactions primarily because it survives longer and can proliferate in tissues?

A. Neutrophil
B. Monocyte/macrophage
C. Eosinophil
D. Mast cell
cards.back:
B — Monocyte/macrophage

Monocytes survive longer than neutrophils and may proliferate after entering tissues.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which condition in the provided text is specifically associated with eosinophil-predominant inflammation?

A. Viral infection
B. Helminthic infection
C. Myocardial infarction
D. Pseudomonas infection
cards.back:
B — Helminthic infection

Eosinophils may predominate in helminthic infections and allergic reactions.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which molecule is stored in endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies and rapidly redistributed to the cell surface after inflammatory stimulation?

A. L-selectin
B. P-selectin
C. LFA-1
D. VCAM-1
cards.back:
B — P-selectin

Histamine and thrombin promote redistribution of P-selectin from Weibel-Palade bodies to the surface.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which endothelial adhesion molecule begins to be expressed within approximately 1–2 hours after TNF/IL-1 stimulation?

A. E-selectin
B. L-selectin
C. MAC-1
D. VLA-4
cards.back:
A — E-selectin

E-selectin and ligands for L-selectin begin to appear within 1–2 hours.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which statement is correct regarding the mannose receptor?

A. It recognizes terminal sialic acid on host cells
B. It is a lectin recognizing terminal mannose and fucose on microbial molecules
C. It is a selectin involved in rolling
D. It is an integrin activated by TNF
cards.back:
B — It is a lectin recognizing terminal mannose and fucose on microbial molecules

This receptor helps distinguish microbial carbohydrates from mammalian terminal sugars.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
A macrophage receptor originally recognized oxidized LDL but also binds microbes. Which receptor class is being described?

A. Selectin
B. Scavenger receptor
C. PECAM-1
D. Mannose-binding lectin
cards.back:
B — Scavenger receptor

Scavenger receptors were originally defined by recognition/endocytosis of oxidized or acetylated LDL and later recognized as microbial-binding receptors as well.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which combination represents the major opsonins specifically identified in the provided text?

A. IgG, C3b, mannose-binding lectin, collectins
B. IgE, C5a, IL-8, LTB4
C. TNF, IL-1, CD31, E-selectin
D. Histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes, serotonin
cards.back:
A — IgG, C3b, mannose-binding lectin, collectins

These four are explicitly identified as major opsonins in the phagocytosis section.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which event occurs last in the classic leukocyte-recruitment sequence?

A. Rolling
B. Integrin activation
C. Stable adhesion
D. Migration toward chemoattractants in tissue
cards.back:
D — Migration toward chemoattractants in tissue

After rolling, activation, stable adhesion, and transmigration, leukocytes migrate through tissues toward chemotactic gradients.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
A patient has severe defects in leukocyte adhesion molecules and recurrent bacterial infections. This observation principally demonstrates that adhesion molecules are:

A. Unimportant to inflammation
B. Critical to host inflammatory defense
C. Relevant only to fibrosis
D. Restricted to lymphocytes
cards.back:
B — Critical to host inflammatory defense

Genetic leukocyte adhesion deficiencies produce increased susceptibility to bacterial infection.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which inflammatory mediator is generated after inflammasome activation according to the provided passage?

A. IL-1
B. IL-8
C. C5a
D. LTB4
cards.back:
A — IL-1

Inflammasome activation induces production of IL-1, which recruits leukocytes.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
A patient with an activating mutation in a receptor develops spontaneous inflammation due to increased IL-1 production. The described disorder belongs to:

A. Autoimmune diseases only
B. Autoinflammatory syndromes
C. Leukocyte adhesion deficiencies
D. Hypersensitivity only
cards.back:
B — Autoinflammatory syndromes

Gain-of-function receptor mutations are described as causing rare autoinflammatory syndromes with spontaneous IL-1 production.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which statement about acute inflammation is most precise?

A. It is always harmful
B. It is rapid, often self-limited, and predominantly neutrophilic
C. It is always caused by bacteria
D. It is invariably followed by fibrosis
cards.back:
B — It is rapid, often self-limited, and predominantly neutrophilic

This captures the specific acute-inflammation pattern emphasized by Robbins.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which statement about chronic inflammation is most precise?

A. It is always preceded by acute inflammation
B. It is associated with agents difficult to eradicate and more tissue destruction/fibrosis
C. It is exclusively neutrophilic
D. It lasts only several hours
cards.back:
B — It is associated with agents difficult to eradicate and more tissue destruction/fibrosis

Chronic inflammation can arise de novo and is associated with persistent difficult-to- eradicate agents, tissue destruction, and fibrosis.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which pairing is incorrect?

A. Gout — urate crystals
B. Atherosclerosis — cholesterol crystals
C. Obesity-associated metabolic syndrome — lipids
D. Alzheimer disease — urate crystals as the named deposit
cards.back:
D — Alzheimer disease — urate crystals as the named deposit

The passage associates Alzheimer disease with amyloid deposits, not urate crystals.

cards.front:
The inflammatory change most directly responsible for erythema and heat is:

A. Stasis
B. Vasodilation with increased blood flow
C. Leukocyte apoptosis
D. Fibrosis
cards.back:
B — Vasodilation with increased blood flow

Increased blood flow resulting from vasodilation causes redness and heat.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which event directly contributes to stasis?

A. Increased vessel diameter and fluid loss
B. Decreased blood viscosity
C. Reduced RBC concentration
D. Increased blood velocity
cards.back:
A — Increased vessel diameter and fluid loss

Fluid loss and vessel dilation produce slower flow, RBC concentration, increased viscosity, and stasis.

— Ultra-high-yield last revision set — part 1

cards.front:
Which pair is correctly matched?

A. L-selectin — endothelium
B. E-selectin — leukocyte
C. P-selectin — platelets and endothelium
D. LFA-1 — endothelial selectin
cards.back:
C — P-selectin — platelets and endothelium

The selectin distribution is a frequent examiner trap.

cards.front:
The final step in elimination of infectious agents and necrotic cells by phagocytes is:

A. Margination
B. Intracellular killing and degradation
C. Rolling
D. Chemotaxis
cards.back:
B — Intracellular killing and degradation

ROS, reactive nitrogen species, and lysosomal enzymes destroy phagocytosed material.

cards.front:
Killing and degradation of microbes by neutrophils and macrophages occur most efficiently:

A. Before phagocytosis
B. After activation of the phagocytes
C. During margination
D. During rolling
cards.back:
B — After activation of the phagocytes

Activation enhances the intracellular microbicidal mechanisms.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Phagocytic killing mechanisms are normally sequestered in:

A. Nuclei
B. Lysosomes
C. Mitochondria
D. Golgi apparatus
cards.back:
B — Lysosomes

Sequestration protects the phagocyte from its own potentially harmful microbicidal substances.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
NADPH oxidase is also called:

A. iNOS
B. Phagocyte oxidase
C. Myeloperoxidase
D. Superoxide dismutase
cards.back:
B — Phagocyte oxidase

NADPH oxidase is the phagocyte oxidase responsible for the respiratory burst.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
NADPH oxidase initially converts oxygen into:

A. Hydrogen peroxide
B. Superoxide anion
C. Hypochlorite
D. Peroxynitrite
cards.back:
B — Superoxide anion

NADPH oxidase uses NADPH to reduce oxygen to superoxide (O₂•⁻).

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
The oxidative reaction triggered in neutrophils during phagocytosis is called:

A. Oxidative phosphorylation
B. Respiratory burst
C. Respiratory failure
D. Oxidative stress response
cards.back:
B — Respiratory burst

The rapid activation of phagocyte oxidase during phagocytosis produces the respiratory burst.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
In resting neutrophils, components of NADPH oxidase are located in:

A. Only the nucleus
B. Plasma membrane and cytoplasm
C. Lysosomes only
D. Mitochondria only
cards.back:
B — Plasma membrane and cytoplasm

Activation causes cytosolic components to translocate to the phagosomal membrane.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
During activation, cytosolic NADPH oxidase components:

A. Enter the nucleus
B. Translocate to the phagosomal membrane
C. Enter mitochondria
D. Are secreted extracellularly
cards.back:
B — Translocate to the phagosomal membrane

Assembly at the phagosomal membrane creates the functional enzyme complex.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
The major advantage of generating ROS within the phagolysosome is:

A. Increased plasma viscosity
B. Destruction of ingested particles while minimizing damage to the host cell
C. Prevention of phagocytosis
D. Activation of fibroblasts
cards.back:
B — Destruction of ingested particles while minimizing damage to the host cell

ROS are compartmentalized within the phagolysosome.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Superoxide is converted mainly into hydrogen peroxide by:

A. Myeloperoxidase
B. Spontaneous dismutation
C. iNOS
D. Catalase
cards.back:
B — Spontaneous dismutation

O₂•⁻ is converted to H₂O₂, largely by spontaneous dismutation.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Hydrogen peroxide alone is:

A. A highly efficient microbicidal substance
B. Unable to efficiently kill microbes by itself
C. The major neutrophil chemoattractant
D. A complement protein
cards.back:
B — Unable to efficiently kill microbes by itself

Its major microbicidal effect is amplified through the MPO-halide system.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Myeloperoxidase is located in neutrophil:

A. Specific granules only
B. Azurophilic granules
C. Cytosol only
D. Nucleus
cards.back:
B — Azurophilic granules

MPO is a major component of primary/azurophilic granules.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
MPO converts H₂O₂ to hypochlorite in the presence of:

A. Fe²⁺
B. Cl⁻
C. NO
D. Arginine
cards.back:
B — Cl⁻

MPO uses a halide, particularly chloride, to generate hypochlorite.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Hypochlorite generated by MPO is chemically analogous to the active ingredient in:

A. Alcohol
B. Household bleach
C. Hydrogen peroxide alone
D. Saline
cards.back:
B — Household bleach

Robbins specifically makes this comparison.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
The most potent bactericidal system of neutrophils described is:

A. NO alone
B. H₂O₂-MPO-halide system
C. C3a-C5a system
D. LTB4 system
cards.back:
B — H₂O₂-MPO-halide system

This system is identified as the most potent bactericidal mechanism of neutrophils.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Hypochlorite destroys microbes primarily by:

A. Inhibiting leukocyte adhesion
B. Halogenation and oxidation of proteins and lipids
C. Inhibiting complement
D. Blocking phagocytosis
cards.back:
B — Halogenation and oxidation of proteins and lipids

These are the mechanisms described for HOCl.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Hydroxyl radical is generated from:

A. H₂O₂
B. C3b
C. NO
D. LTB4
cards.back:
A — H₂O₂

H₂O₂ is converted to the highly destructive hydroxyl radical.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Oxygen-derived free radicals damage:

A. Lipids only
B. Proteins only
C. Nucleic acids only
D. Lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids
cards.back:
D — Lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids

ROS modify all three classes of cellular macromolecules.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Nitric oxide is produced from:

A. Glucose
B. Arginine
C. Cholesterol
D. Linoleic acid
cards.back:
B — Arginine

NOS enzymes generate NO from arginine.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Which NOS is principally involved in microbial killing?

A. eNOS
B. nNOS
C. iNOS
D. COX-2
cards.back:
C — iNOS

Inducible NOS is the NOS involved in antimicrobial activity.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
eNOS and nNOS are:

A. Induced only during infection
B. Constitutively expressed at low levels
C. Restricted to macrophages
D. Located exclusively in lysosomes
cards.back:
B — Constitutively expressed at low levels

Their products serve vascular and neural functions, respectively.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
NO produced by eNOS primarily helps maintain:

A. Vascular tone
B. Bacterial phagocytosis
C. Platelet production
D. Fibrosis
cards.back:
A — Vascular tone

eNOS-derived NO regulates vascular tone.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
NO produced by nNOS primarily functions as:

A. A neurotransmitter
B. An opsonin
C. A complement protein
D. A growth factor
cards.back:
A — A neurotransmitter

nNOS-derived NO has a neurotransmitter role.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
iNOS is induced in macrophages by:

A. IFN-γ and microbial products
B. Albumin and collagen
C. IgG alone
D. Histamine alone
cards.back:
A — IFN-γ and microbial products

Cytokines such as IFN-γ and microbial products induce iNOS.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
In macrophages, NO reacts with superoxide to produce:

A. Hypochlorite
B. Peroxynitrite
C. LTB4
D. C5a
cards.back:
B — Peroxynitrite

NO + O₂•⁻ produces highly reactive peroxynitrite.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
The strongest evidence for overlapping ROS and RNS functions is that:

A. Both oxidases are identical
B. Mice deficient in either pathway alone are only mildly susceptible, whereas deficiency of both causes severe infection
C. Both pathways occur only in neutrophils
D. Neither pathway contributes to microbial killing
cards.back:
B — Mice deficient in either pathway alone are only mildly susceptible, whereas deficiency of both causes severe infection

The text uses knockout mice to demonstrate functional redundancy.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Besides antimicrobial activity, NO:

A. Causes vasoconstriction
B. Relaxes vascular smooth muscle and promotes vasodilation
C. Activates platelets
D. Inhibits endothelial function
cards.back:
B — Relaxes vascular smooth muscle and promotes vasodilation

Vasodilation is an additional effect of NO.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Acid proteases primarily degrade:

A. Extracellular collagen
B. Bacteria and debris within phagolysosomes
C. Platelets
D. Antibodies
cards.back:
B — Bacteria and debris within phagolysosomes

Acid proteases act in the acidified phagolysosome.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Phagolysosomes are acidified by:

A. Sodium channels
B. Membrane-bound proton pumps
C. COX enzymes
D. Selectins
cards.back:
B — Membrane-bound proton pumps

Proton pumps create the acidic environment required for acid proteases.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Neutral proteases can degrade all of the following EXCEPT:

A. Collagen
B. Elastin
C. Fibrin
D. Immunoglobulin as the specifically listed major target
cards.back:
D — Immunoglobulin as the specifically listed major target

The listed extracellular substrates include collagen, basement membrane, fibrin, elastin, and cartilage.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Neutral proteases contribute to tissue injury mainly by degrading:

A. Extracellular tissue components
B. Nuclear DNA only
C. Antibodies only
D. RBC membranes only
cards.back:
A — Extracellular tissue components

Their extracellular proteolytic activity contributes to inflammatory tissue destruction.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Neutrophil elastase can help combat bacterial infection by degrading:

A. Host collagen only
B. Bacterial virulence factors
C. Complement receptors
D. Cytokines exclusively
cards.back:
B — Bacterial virulence factors

This is a specific antimicrobial function described for elastase.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
The major inhibitor of neutrophil elastase is:

A. α1-antitrypsin
B. α2-macroglobulin only
C. C3b
D. MPO
cards.back:
A — α1-antitrypsin

α1-antitrypsin is identified as the major neutrophil elastase inhibitor.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
α1-antitrypsin deficiency increases the risk of:

A. Asthma due to histamine
B. Emphysema due to uncontrolled elastase activity
C. Gout
D. Peptic ulcer
cards.back:
B — Emphysema due to uncontrolled elastase activity

Excess elastase destroys elastic support fibers in the lung.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Another antiprotease mentioned is:

A. α2-macroglobulin
B. C5a
C. IL-17
D. TNF
cards.back:
A — α2-macroglobulin

α2-macroglobulin is another antiprotease in serum and secretions.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Defensins are:

A. Cationic arginine-rich antimicrobial peptides
B. Complement proteins
C. Prostaglandins
D. Selectins
cards.back:
A — Cationic arginine-rich antimicrobial peptides

Defensins are microbicidal granule contents.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Lysozyme hydrolyzes the:

A. Peptide bond in collagen
B. Muramic acid–N-acetylglucosamine bond
C. Phosphodiester bond in DNA
D. Ester bond of triglycerides
cards.back:
B — Muramic acid–N-acetylglucosamine bond

This bond occurs in the glycopeptide coat of bacteria.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Lactoferrin is primarily an:

A. Iron-binding protein
B. Antibody
C. Complement component
D. Integrin
cards.back:
A — Iron-binding protein

Lactoferrin is present in specific granules.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Major basic protein is found characteristically in:

A. Neutrophils
B. Eosinophils
C. Macrophages
D. T lymphocytes
cards.back:
B — Eosinophils

Major basic protein is a cationic eosinophil protein toxic to many helminthic parasites.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Compared with macrophages, neutrophils have a:

A. More prolonged, transcription-dependent response
B. Rapid, short-lived response dominated by degranulation and enzymatic activity
C. Predominantly cytokine-secretory response
D. Years-long lifespan in tissues
cards.back:
B — Rapid, short-lived response dominated by degranulation and enzymatic activity

Table 3.4 contrasts the rapid neutrophil response with the prolonged macrophage response.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Tissue-resident macrophages may survive for:

A. Hours
B. Several days
C. Years
D. Only minutes
cards.back:
C — Years

Table 3.4 lists tissue-resident macrophages as having lifespans of years.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Compared with neutrophils, macrophages show:

A. More prominent nitric oxide production
B. Less prominent NO production
C. No cytokine production
D. No gene transcription
cards.back:
A — More prominent nitric oxide production

Macrophage NO is induced following transcriptional activation of iNOS.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
NET formation is a feature of:

A. Neutrophils but not macrophages
B. Macrophages but not neutrophils
C. Both equally
D. Neither
cards.back:
A — Neutrophils but not macrophages

Table 3.4 lists rapid NET formation in neutrophils and no NET formation in macrophages.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
Which is a functional similarity between neutrophils and macrophages?

A. Identical lifespan
B. Phagocytosis
C. Identical cytokine production
D. Identical ROS production
cards.back:
B — Phagocytosis

Both cell types phagocytose, migrate through vessels, and undergo chemotaxis.

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front: Describe the respiratory burst.
cards.back:
Activation of NADPH oxidase assembles the phagocyte oxidase complex at the phagosomal membrane, reducing oxygen to superoxide; superoxide generates H₂O₂ and, through MPO and chloride, hypochlorite.

Key points:
• NADPH oxidase
• Superoxide
• Respiratory burst
• H₂O₂
• MPO
• Hypochlorite

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front: Compare neutrophils and macrophages.
cards.back:
Neutrophils respond rapidly and are short-lived, with prominent degranulation, ROS generation, and NET formation; macrophages respond more slowly and persist longer, with greater NO and cytokine production and important roles in repair.

Key points:
• Lifespan
• Speed of response
• ROS
• NO
• Cytokines
• NETs
• Repair

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front: Describe the role of lysosomal enzymes in inflammation.
cards.back:
Acid proteases degrade ingested microbes/debris within phagolysosomes, whereas neutral proteases can degrade extracellular matrix and contribute to tissue destruction; antiproteases normally restrict this damage.

Key points:
• Acid proteases
• Neutral proteases
• Tissue destruction
• α1-antitrypsin
• α2-macroglobulin

— Intracellular destruction of microbes and debris

cards.front:
NETs are:

A. Intracellular lysosomal granules
B. Extracellular fibrillar networks that trap microbes
C. Complement complexes
D. Collagen fibers
cards.back:
B — Extracellular fibrillar networks that trap microbes

NETs concentrate antimicrobial substances and limit microbial spread.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
NETs are produced mainly in response to:

A. Bacteria and fungi
B. Only viruses
C. Only parasites
D. Only allergens
cards.back:
A — Bacteria and fungi

Infectious pathogens, particularly bacteria and fungi, are major stimuli.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
NET formation may also be induced by:

A. Chemokines, cytokines, complement proteins, and ROS
B. Albumin alone
C. Collagen alone
D. Fibronectin only
cards.back:
A — Chemokines, cytokines, complement proteins, and ROS

These inflammatory mediators are specifically listed as NET stimuli.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
NETs consist primarily of a viscous meshwork of:

A. Collagen
B. Nuclear chromatin
C. Fibrin
D. Elastin
cards.back:
B — Nuclear chromatin

Nuclear chromatin forms the structural framework that traps microbes.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
NETs concentrate:

A. Granule antimicrobial peptides and enzymes
B. Only antibodies
C. Only complement proteins
D. Plasma proteins only
cards.back:
A — Granule antimicrobial peptides and enzymes

Granule proteins bind to the chromatin meshwork.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
NET formation begins with ROS-dependent activation of an arginine deaminase that converts:

A. Arginine to citrulline
B. Citrulline to arginine
C. Lysine to arginine
D. Arginine to lysine
cards.back:
A — Arginine to citrulline

This modification contributes to chromatin decondensation.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
During NET formation, MPO and elastase:

A. Remain entirely extracellular
B. Enter the nucleus and promote chromatin decondensation
C. Inhibit chromatin release
D. Destroy the cell membrane only
cards.back:
B — Enter the nucleus and promote chromatin decondensation

Nuclear entry of these enzymes contributes to chromatin release.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
NET formation ultimately causes:

A. Nuclear envelope rupture and chromatin release
B. Nuclear replication
C. Increased neutrophil lifespan
D. Complete inhibition of microbial trapping
cards.back:
A — Nuclear envelope rupture and chromatin release

Release of nuclear chromatin forms the extracellular trap.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
During NET formation, the neutrophil:

A. Retains its nucleus and proliferates
B. Loses its nucleus and dies
C. Converts into a macrophage
D. Becomes a plasma cell
cards.back:
B — Loses its nucleus and dies

NET formation is associated with neutrophil death.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
NETs have been detected in the blood during:

A. Sepsis
B. Simple edema
C. Uncomplicated fracture
D. Normal physiology only
cards.back:
A — Sepsis

Circulating NETs have been observed during sepsis.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
The nuclear chromatin itself contributes:

A. A major increase in infection susceptibility
B. Only a minimal increase in infection susceptibility
C. Complete immunity
D. No microbicidal redundancy
cards.back:
B — Only a minimal increase in infection susceptibility

This supports the redundancy of leukocyte microbicidal mechanisms.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Leukocytes can damage normal tissues during:

A. Normal antimicrobial defense with collateral damage
B. Autoimmune disease
C. Allergic disease
D. All of the above
cards.back:
D — All of the above

All three circumstances are explicitly described.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
In some difficult-to-eradicate infections, tissue pathology may be caused more by:

A. The microbe itself than the host response
B. The prolonged host response than the microbe itself
C. Fibroblasts alone
D. Platelets alone
cards.back:
B — The prolonged host response than the microbe itself

Tuberculosis and certain viral diseases are examples.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
The mechanisms used by leukocytes for host tissue injury are:

A. Completely different from antimicrobial mechanisms
B. The same as antimicrobial effector mechanisms
C. Limited to antibody secretion
D. Limited to chemotaxis
cards.back:
B — The same as antimicrobial effector mechanisms

Once activated, leukocyte effector mechanisms do not distinguish offender from host.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Which trio represents important leukocyte-derived tissue-damaging substances?

A. ROS, NO, lysosomal enzymes
B. IgG, IgE, IgM
C. C1, C2, C3
D. Collagen, elastin, fibrin
cards.back:
A — ROS, NO, lysosomal enzymes

These are released during activation/phagocytosis and can injure host tissue.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Frustrated phagocytosis occurs when:

A. A leukocyte easily ingests a small bacterium
B. A phagocyte encounters material too large or difficult to engulf
C. A leukocyte lacks selectins
D. Complement is absent
cards.back:
B — A phagocyte encounters material too large or difficult to engulf

Large immune-complex deposits are specifically mentioned.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
A classic example of material causing frustrated phagocytosis is:

A. Immune complexes deposited on a large surface such as the glomerular basement membrane
B. Albumin in plasma
C. Small bacteria
D. Soluble cytokines
cards.back:
A — Immune complexes deposited on a large surface such as the glomerular basement membrane

Such material cannot be surrounded and ingested effectively.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Frustrated phagocytosis leads to:

A. Strong leukocyte activation and extracellular release of lysosomal enzymes
B. Immediate leukocyte apoptosis without enzyme release
C. Reduced inflammation
D. Fibrosis without inflammation
cards.back:
A — Strong leukocyte activation and extracellular release of lysosomal enzymes

The inability to ingest the material produces extracellular enzyme release.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Urate crystals can cause lysosomal enzyme release because they:

A. Activate C1 directly
B. Damage the phagolysosomal membrane
C. Inhibit phagocytosis completely
D. Destroy leukocyte nuclei directly
cards.back:
B — Damage the phagolysosomal membrane

Membrane disruption releases granule contents.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Activated macrophages can produce growth factors that stimulate:

A. Endothelial cells and fibroblasts
B. RBCs only
C. Neutrophils only
D. Platelets only
cards.back:
A — Endothelial cells and fibroblasts

These factors support proliferation and collagen synthesis during repair.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Macrophages contribute to connective-tissue remodeling through:

A. Enzymes that remodel connective tissue
B. Selectins alone
C. IgE production
D. C3b cleavage alone
cards.back:
A — Enzymes that remodel connective tissue

Macrophages have important remodeling functions in repair.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Some T lymphocytes contribute to acute inflammation mainly through production of:

A. IL-17
B. IgG
C. C3b
D. LTB4
cards.back:
A — IL-17

Th17 cells and their IL-17 response are specifically highlighted.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
IL-17 promotes acute inflammation by inducing secretion of:

A. Chemokines that recruit other leukocytes
B. Antibodies only
C. Fibronectin only
D. Complement inhibitors
cards.back:
A — Chemokines that recruit other leukocytes

This is the key inflammatory role described for IL-17.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Effective Th17 responses are particularly important for protection against:

A. Fungal and bacterial infections
B. Only helminths
C. Only viral hepatitis
D. Only autoimmune disease
cards.back:
A — Fungal and bacterial infections

Defective Th17 responses increase susceptibility to fungal and bacterial infections.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Individuals lacking effective Th17 responses may develop “cold abscesses,” which characteristically lack:

A. Fibrosis and granulomas
B. Warmth and redness
C. Macrophages
D. Bacteria
cards.back:
B — Warmth and redness

These abscesses lack classic acute inflammatory warmth and redness.

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front: Describe NET formation.
cards.back:
ROS activate an arginine deaminase, causing arginine-to-citrulline conversion and chromatin decondensation; MPO and elastase enter the nucleus, nuclear envelope rupture occurs, and chromatin containing antimicrobial proteins is extruded extracellularly, causing neutrophil death.

Key points:
• ROS-dependent initiation
• ROS-dependent initiation
• Citrullination
• Chromatin decondensation
• MPO/elastase
• Nuclear rupture
• Neutrophil death

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front: What is frustrated phagocytosis?
cards.back:
It is strong leukocyte activation with extracellular release of lysosomal enzymes when phagocytes encounter material they cannot effectively engulf.

Key points:
• Inability to engulf
• Strong activation
• Extracellular enzyme release
• Tissue injury
• Immune complexes as example

— Neutrophil extracellular traps and leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

cards.front:
Which is the major reason inflammation declines after the offending stimulus is removed?

A. Mediators continue indefinitely
B. Mediators have short half-lives and are degraded/inactivated
C. Leukocytes proliferate continuously
D. Endothelial cells become permanently activated
cards.back:
B — Mediators have short half-lives and are degraded/inactivated

Short mediator half-lives contribute to termination.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Most neutrophils in tissues die:

A. By necrosis after weeks
B. By apoptosis within several hours after leaving blood
C. By differentiation into macrophages
D. Only after fibrosis
cards.back:
B — By apoptosis within several hours after leaving blood

Short neutrophil survival contributes to resolution.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
An active termination mechanism involves switching from:

A. Prostaglandins to thromboxanes
B. Leukotrienes to lipoxins
C. Histamine to serotonin
D. C5a to C3b
cards.back:
B — Leukotrienes to lipoxins

The eicosanoid profile changes from proinflammatory leukotrienes to antiinflammatory lipoxins.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Which pair consists of antiinflammatory cytokines involved in termination?

A. TNF and IL-1
B. TGF-β and IL-10
C. IL-17 and IFN-γ
D. C3a and C5a
cards.back:
B — TGF-β and IL-10

Both are released by macrophages and other cells during active termination.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Experimental neural control of inflammation includes:

A. Cholinergic discharge inhibiting macrophage TNF production
B. Dopamine stimulating TNF
C. Acetylcholine stimulating ROS production
D. Sensory nerve destruction increasing TNF
cards.back:
A — Cholinergic discharge inhibiting macrophage TNF production

Neural stop signals are described as an experimental antiinflammatory mechanism.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
The principal mediators of acute inflammation include:

A. Vasoactive amines, lipid mediators, cytokines/chemokines, and complement products
B. Only cytokines
C. Only antibodies
D. Only complement
cards.back:
A — Vasoactive amines, lipid mediators, cytokines/chemokines, and complement products

These are the major classes listed in the text and Table 3.5.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Cell-derived mediators may be:

A. Stored in intracellular granules or synthesized de novo
B. Produced only in the liver
C. Produced only by neutrophils
D. Always plasma-derived
cards.back:
A — Stored in intracellular granules or synthesized de novo

Histamine is stored; prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and cytokines are synthesized after stimulation.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
The major sentinel cells producing acute inflammatory mediators are:

A. Macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells
B. RBCs, platelets, fibroblasts
C. Plasma cells only
D. Hepatocytes only
cards.back:
A — Macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells

These cells detect invaders and tissue damage.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Which statement about inflammatory mediators is correct?

A. They remain active indefinitely
B. Most are short-lived
C. They all have identical effects
D. They cannot stimulate one another
cards.back:
B — Most are short-lived

Rapid decay, enzymatic inactivation, scavenging, and inhibition help control their effects.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Complement products can stimulate release of:

A. Histamine
B. Collagen
C. DNA
D. Albumin
cards.back:
A — Histamine

Complement activation products can induce mast-cell histamine release.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
TNF can stimulate endothelial cells to produce:

A. IL-1 and chemokines
B. IgG
C. C3b only
D. α1-antitrypsin
cards.back:
A — IL-1 and chemokines

Secondary mediator release amplifies the inflammatory cascade.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
The two major vasoactive amines are:

A. Histamine and serotonin
B. TNF and IL-1
C. C3a and C5a
D. Bradykinin and LTB4
cards.back:
A — Histamine and serotonin

Both are preformed mediators with important vascular effects.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
The richest source of histamine is:

A. Platelets
B. Mast cells
C. Neutrophils
D. Endothelial cells
cards.back:
B — Mast cells

Mast cells adjacent to blood vessels are the richest source.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Histamine is stored primarily in:

A. Mast-cell granules
B. Nuclei
C. Mitochondria
D. Extracellular matrix
cards.back:
A — Mast-cell granules

It is rapidly released by mast-cell degranulation.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Which complement products trigger mast-cell histamine release?

A. C3a and C5a
B. C3b and C5b
C. C1 and C2
D. C6–C9
cards.back:
A — C3a and C5a

These are the complement anaphylatoxins named in the text.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Histamine causes:

A. Arteriolar dilation and venular permeability increase
B. Only venular constriction
C. Platelet destruction
D. Fibrosis
cards.back:
A — Arteriolar dilation and venular permeability increase

These are its principal vascular effects.

— Termination of acute inflammation and mediators

cards.front:
Histamine is the principal mediator of:

A. Delayed prolonged leakage lasting days
B. Immediate transient vascular permeability increase

C3 convertase splits C3 into:

A. C1a and C1b
B. C3a and C3b
C. C4a and C4b
D. C5a and C5b
cards.back:
B — C3a and C3b

— Complement system

cards.front:
C3a primarily acts as:

A. An opsonin deposited on microbes
B. An anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation
C. The MAC
D. A T-cell receptor
cards.back:
B — An anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation

— Complement system

cards.front:
C3b becomes:

A. Covalently attached to the target cell/molecule
B. A neurotransmitter
C. A selectin
D. A kinin
cards.back:
A — Covalently attached to the target cell/molecule

— Complement system

cards.front:
C5 convertase cleaves:

A. C1
B. C3
C. C5
D. C9
cards.back:
C — C5

— Complement system

cards.front:
C5 cleavage produces:

A. C5a and C5b
B. C3a and C3b
C. C4a and C4b
D. C6 and C7
cards.back:
A — C5a and C5b

— Complement system

cards.front:
C5b binds:

A. C1–C3
B. C6–C9
C. IgG
D. Histamine
cards.back:
B — C6–C9

— Complement system

cards.front:
The membrane attack complex consists of multiple molecules of:

A. C3b
B. C5a
C. C9
D. C1
cards.back:
C — C9

— Complement system

cards.front:
Which complement products act as anaphylatoxins?

A. C3a, C5a, and to a lesser extent C4a
B. C3b only
C. C5b only
D. C6–C9
cards.back:
A — C3a, C5a, and to a lesser extent C4a

— Complement system

cards.front:
C5a is chemotactic for:

A. Neutrophils only
B. Neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils
C. RBCs only
D. Fibroblasts only
cards.back:
B — Neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils

— Complement system

cards.front:
C5a also activates:

A. Lipoxygenase pathways in neutrophils and monocytes
B. COX-1 only
C. iNOS in RBCs
D. Collagenase in fibroblasts only
cards.back:
A — Lipoxygenase pathways in neutrophils and monocytes

— Complement system

cards.front:
C3b and iC3b function as:

A. Anaphylatoxins
B. Opsonins
C. Cytokines
D. Kinins
cards.back:
B — Opsonins

— Complement system

cards.front:
Complement-mediated lysis is particularly important against:

A. Neisseria
B. Mycobacteria
C. Fungi only
D. Helminths only
cards.back:
A — Neisseria

— Complement system

cards.front:
Deficiency of terminal complement components predisposes particularly to:

A. Neisseria infections
B. Viral infections only
C. Helminth infections
D. Autoimmune thyroiditis
cards.back:
A — Neisseria infections

— Complement system

cards.front:
C1 inhibitor blocks:

A. C3 cleavage
B. Activation of C1
C. MAC formation directly
D. C5a binding
cards.back:
B — Activation of C1

— Complement system

cards.front:
Inherited deficiency of C1 inhibitor causes:

A. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
B. Hereditary angioedema
C. Atypical HUS
D. CGD
cards.back:
B — Hereditary angioedema

— Complement system

cards.front:
DAF primarily prevents:

A. Formation of C3 convertases
B. Formation of antibodies
C. Histamine release
D. NET formation
cards.back:
A — Formation of C3 convertases

— Complement system

cards.front:
CD59 inhibits formation of:

A. C3 convertase
B. Membrane attack complex
C. C5 convertase
D. C1 complex
cards.back:
B — Membrane attack complex

— Complement system

cards.front:
DAF and CD59 are attached to plasma membranes by:

A. Disulfide bonds
B. GPI anchors
C. Integrins
D. Selectins
cards.back:
B — GPI anchors

— Complement system

cards.front:
An acquired defect in GPI-anchor formation leads to deficiency of DAF/CD59 and causes:

A. CGD
B. PNH
C. Hereditary angioedema
D. SLE
cards.back:
B — PNH

Loss of complement regulatory proteins makes RBCs susceptible to complement- mediated lysis.

— Complement system

cards.front:
Factor H primarily inhibits:

A. Classical complement activation
B. Alternative pathway activation
C. Histamine release
D. Leukocyte rolling
cards.back:
B — Alternative pathway activation

— Complement system

cards.front:
Factor H promotes:

A. Cleavage/destruction of C3b and turnover of C3 convertases
B. C5a chemotaxis
C. MAC assembly
D. Histamine synthesis
cards.back:
A — Cleavage/destruction of C3b and turnover of C3 convertases

— Complement system

cards.front:
Inherited defects in Factor H can cause an atypical form of:

A. Hemolytic uremic syndrome
B. Asthma
C. Peptic ulcer
D. Rheumatoid arthritis
cards.back:
A — Hemolytic uremic syndrome

— Complement system

cards.front:
Factor H polymorphisms have also been linked to:

A. Age-related macular degeneration
B. Asthma
C. Gout
D. Psoriasis
cards.back:
A — Age-related macular degeneration

— Complement system

cards.front: Describe the three complement activation pathways.
cards.back:
The classical pathway is triggered by C1 binding antigen-bound IgM/IgG; the alternative pathway is triggered by microbial surfaces such as LPS without antibody; the lectin pathway is triggered by mannose-binding lectin binding microbial carbohydrates. All form C3 convertase.

Key points:
• Classical
• Alternative
• Lectin
• Trigger
• C3 convertase

— Complement system

cards.front: State the three major functions of complement.
cards.back:
1. Inflammation 2. Opsonization and phagocytosis 3. Cell lysis through the membrane attack complex

Key points:
• C3a/C5a → inflammation
• C3b/iC3b → opsonization
• C5b–C9 → MAC-mediated lysis

— Complement system

cards.front:
Platelet-activating factor is derived from:

A. Phospholipids
B. Proteins
C. DNA
D. Cholesterol only
cards.back:
A — Phospholipids

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
PAF was initially discovered as a factor that caused:

A. Platelet aggregation
B. Leukocyte apoptosis
C. Fibrosis
D. Fever
cards.back:
A — Platelet aggregation

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Which cells can produce PAF?

A. Platelets, basophils, mast cells, neutrophils, macrophages, endothelial cells
B. Only platelets
C. Only macrophages
D. Only fibroblasts
cards.back:
A — Platelets, basophils, mast cells, neutrophils, macrophages, endothelial cells

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
PAF can cause all of the following EXCEPT:

A. Vasoconstriction
B. Bronchoconstriction
C. Vasodilation at low concentrations
D. Decreased vascular permeability at low concentrations
cards.back:
D — Decreased vascular permeability at low concentrations

Low concentrations produce vasodilation and increased venular permeability.

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Despite multiple inflammatory effects, PAF antagonists:

A. Have proven universally effective
B. Have not been useful in various inflammatory diseases
C. Cure asthma
D. Prevent all platelet aggregation
cards.back:
B — Have not been useful in various inflammatory diseases

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Protease-activated receptors (PARs) on leukocytes are activated by:

A. Thrombin
B. Histamine
C. C3b
D. TNF
cards.back:
A — Thrombin

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Thrombin converts:

A. Fibrin into fibrinogen
B. Fibrinogen into fibrin
C. C3 into C3a
D. Kininogen into collagen
cards.back:
B — Fibrinogen into fibrin

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Fibrinopeptides may:

A. Stimulate inflammation
B. Inhibit all inflammation
C. Produce antibodies
D. Cause granulomas directly
cards.back:
A — Stimulate inflammation

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
The relationship between coagulation and inflammation is difficult to interpret because:

A. They never occur together
B. Many tissue injuries involve both clotting and inflammation
C. Thrombin has no biological role
D. Fibrin is never inflammatory
cards.back:
B — Many tissue injuries involve both clotting and inflammation

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Kinins are derived from:

A. Kininogens
B. Immunoglobulins
C. Complement
D. Arachidonic acid
cards.back:
A — Kininogens

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Kininogens are cleaved by:

A. Kallikreins
B. COX enzymes
C. Lipoxygenases
D. MPO
cards.back:
A — Kallikreins

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Bradykinin causes:

A. Increased vascular permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, vasodilation, and pain
B. Only vasoconstriction
C. Only platelet aggregation
D. Only fever
cards.back:
A — Increased vascular permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, vasodilation, and pain

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Bradykinin is short-lived because it is rapidly inactivated by:

A. Kininase
B. COX-2
C. MPO
D. DAF
cards.back:
A — Kininase

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Neuropeptides are secreted by:

A. Sensory nerves and various leukocytes
B. RBCs only
C. Platelets only
D. Hepatocytes only
cards.back:
A — Sensory nerves and various leukocytes

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Substance P is particularly prominent in nerve fibers in the:

A. Lung and gastrointestinal tract
B. Kidney only
C. Bone marrow only
D. Skin only
cards.back:
A — Lung and gastrointestinal tract

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Substance P contributes to inflammation by:

A. Transmitting pain and increasing vascular permeability
B. Inhibiting pain
C. Blocking leukocyte migration
D. Inhibiting vascular permeability
cards.back:
A — Transmitting pain and increasing vascular permeability

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Activation of the efferent vagus nerve can suppress inflammation by inhibiting production of:

A. TNF
B. C3b
C. Histamine
D. LTB4
cards.back:
A — TNF

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Clinical trials of vagus nerve stimulation were mentioned for:

A. Rheumatoid arthritis
B. Peptic ulcer
C. Osteomyelitis only
D. Asthma only
cards.back:
A — Rheumatoid arthritis

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
The major mediator of vasodilation listed in Table 3.8 is:

A. Histamine
B. C5b
C. Bradykinin only
D. LTB4 only
cards.back:
A — Histamine

Prostaglandins are also listed for vasodilation.

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
The principal mediators of fever include:

A. IL-1, TNF, and prostaglandins
B. Histamine only
C. C3b only
D. LTB4 only
cards.back:
A — IL-1, TNF, and prostaglandins

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Pain is mediated by:

A. Prostaglandins, bradykinin, and substance P
B. C3b only
C. LTB4 only
D. TNF only
cards.back:
A — Prostaglandins, bradykinin, and substance P

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
Tissue damage is mediated particularly by:

A. Lysosomal enzymes and ROS
B. PGI₂ only
C. C3b only
D. Histamine only
cards.back:
A — Lysosomal enzymes and ROS

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front: List the major actions of bradykinin.
cards.back:
Bradykinin increases vascular permeability, causes smooth-muscle contraction and vasodilation, and produces pain.

Key points:
• Permeability
• Smooth-muscle contraction
• Vasodilation
• Pain
• Rapid inactivation by kininase

— Other mediators of inflammation

cards.front:
The general morphologic hallmarks of acute inflammation are:

A. Vessel dilation and accumulation of leukocytes and fluid extravascularly
B. Granuloma formation only
C. Fibrosis only
D. Vessel thrombosis only
cards.back:
A — Vessel dilation and accumulation of leukocytes and fluid extravascularly

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Recognition of specific morphologic patterns is important because they may:

A. Identify the underlying cause
B. Always determine prognosis
C. Eliminate the need for clinical examination
D. Prove malignancy
cards.back:
A — Identify the underlying cause

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Serous inflammation is characterized by:

A. Cell-rich pus
B. Exudation of cell-poor fluid
C. Dense fibrosis
D. Granuloma formation
cards.back:
B — Exudation of cell-poor fluid

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Serous inflammation typically contains:

A. Large numbers of leukocytes and microbes
B. Little cellular material and usually no microbes
C. Only RBCs
D. Only fibrin
cards.back:
B — Little cellular material and usually no microbes

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Serous inflammation may occur in cavities lined by:

A. Peritoneum, pleura, or pericardium
B. Bone marrow only
C. Synovium only
D. Endothelium only
cards.back:
A — Peritoneum, pleura, or pericardium

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Accumulation of fluid in a serous cavity is called:

A. Abscess
B. Effusion
C. Organization
D. Ulcer
cards.back:
B — Effusion

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Effusions can occur:

A. Only in inflammatory disease
B. Also in noninflammatory conditions
C. Only during infection
D. Only after burns
cards.back:
B — Also in noninflammatory conditions

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
A skin blister after a burn represents:

A. Fibrinous inflammation
B. Serous fluid accumulation within/immediately beneath damaged epidermis
C. Purulent inflammation
D. Granulomatous inflammation
cards.back:
B — Serous fluid accumulation within/immediately beneath damaged epidermis

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Fibrinous inflammation occurs when:

A. Vascular permeability increases enough for fibrinogen to escape
B. Vascular permeability decreases
C. No plasma proteins leave blood
D. Only RBCs escape
cards.back:
A — Vascular permeability increases enough for fibrinogen to escape

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Fibrin is deposited in the:

A. Extracellular space
B. Nucleus
C. Mitochondria
D. Lysosome
cards.back:
A — Extracellular space

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Fibrinous exudates are characteristic of inflammation involving:

A. Body-cavity linings such as meninges, pericardium, and pleura
B. Bone marrow only
C. Skeletal muscle only
D. Kidney glomeruli only
cards.back:
A — Body-cavity linings such as meninges, pericardium, and pleura

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Histologically, fibrin typically appears as:

A. Basophilic amorphous globules
B. Eosinophilic meshwork of threads or an amorphous coagulum
C. Clear vacuoles
D. Sheets of plasma cells
cards.back:
B — Eosinophilic meshwork of threads or an amorphous coagulum

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Fibrinous exudate can be cleared by:

A. Fibrinolysis and macrophages
B. Only neutrophil apoptosis
C. Only antibodies
D. Only eosinophils
cards.back:
A — Fibrinolysis and macrophages

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Failure to remove fibrin over time can lead to:

A. Organization and scarring
B. Complete resolution always
C. Immediate pus formation
D. Leukopenia
cards.back:
A — Organization and scarring

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Extensive fibrosis in the pericardium may result in:

A. Obliteration of the pericardial space
B. Increased pericardial fluid only
C. Bronchospasm
D. Ulceration
cards.back:
A — Obliteration of the pericardial space Purulent inflammation and abscess

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Purulent inflammation is characterized by:

A. Pus production
B. Pure transudate formation
C. Granuloma formation
D. Only fibrin deposition
cards.back:
A — Pus production

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Pus contains:

A. Neutrophils, liquefied necrotic debris, and edema fluid
B. Only RBCs
C. Only plasma proteins
D. Only macrophages
cards.back:
A — Neutrophils, liquefied necrotic debris, and edema fluid

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
The most frequent cause of purulent inflammation is:

A. Pyogenic bacterial infection
B. Viral infection
C. Hypoxia
D. Autoimmunity
cards.back:
A — Pyogenic bacterial infection

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Staphylococci are cited as bacteria that cause:

A. Caseous necrosis
B. Liquefactive tissue necrosis
C. Fat necrosis
D. Fibrinoid necrosis
cards.back:
B — Liquefactive tissue necrosis

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
A common example of acute suppurative inflammation is:

A. Acute appendicitis
B. Tuberculosis
C. Rheumatoid arthritis
D. Atherosclerosis
cards.back:
A — Acute appendicitis

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
An abscess is:

A. A diffuse collection of transudate
B. A localized collection of pus
C. A granuloma without necrosis
D. A serous effusion
cards.back:
B — A localized collection of pus

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
The center of an abscess usually contains:

A. Viable neutrophils only
B. Liquefied necrotic leukocytes and tissue cells
C. Dense collagen
D. Mature fibroblasts only
cards.back:
B — Liquefied necrotic leukocytes and tissue cells

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Surrounding the necrotic center of an abscess there is usually:

A. A zone of preserved neutrophils
B. Only lymphocytes
C. Only collagen
D. Only eosinophils
cards.back:
A — A zone of preserved neutrophils

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Peripheral to the neutrophilic zone there may be:

A. Vascular dilation and parenchymal/fibroblastic proliferation
B. Only necrosis
C. Only RBC destruction
D. No tissue response
cards.back:
A — Vascular dilation and parenchymal/fibroblastic proliferation

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
An ulcer is:

A. A localized surface defect caused by sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue
B. A cystic cavity filled with serum
C. A granuloma
D. A collection of pus
cards.back:
A — A localized surface defect caused by sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Ulceration requires:

A. Tissue necrosis and inflammation on or near a surface
B. Only fibrosis
C. Only vasodilation
D. Only infection
cards.back:
A — Tissue necrosis and inflammation on or near a surface

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Common mucosal sites for ulcers include all EXCEPT:

A. Mouth
B. Stomach
C. Intestine
D. Lung alveoli
cards.back:
D — Lung alveoli

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Lower-extremity ulcers are especially common in people with:

A. Vascular insufficiency-associated disorders such as diabetes and sickle cell anemia
B. Asthma
C. Hyperthyroidism
D. Migraine
cards.back:
A — Vascular insufficiency-associated disorders such as diabetes and sickle cell anemia

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
The classic example of an ulcer in the text is:

A. Peptic ulcer
B. Abscess
C. Fibrinous pericarditis
D. Skin blister
cards.back:
A — Peptic ulcer

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
In the acute stage of peptic ulceration, the margins show:

A. Intense polymorphonuclear infiltration and vascular dilation
B. Dense collagen and no inflammation
C. Only eosinophils
D. Granulomas
cards.back:
A — Intense polymorphonuclear infiltration and vascular dilation

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
With chronicity, an ulcer develops:

A. Fibroblastic proliferation, scarring, lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells
B. Only neutrophils
C. Only fibrin
D. Only eosinophils
cards.back:
A — Fibroblastic proliferation, scarring, lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front: Compare serous, fibrinous, and purulent inflammation.
cards.back:
• Serous: cell-poor fluid • Fibrinous: fibrin-rich exudate from marked permeability increase • Purulent: pus containing neutrophils and necrotic debris, usually due to pyogenic bacteria.

Key points:
• Nature of exudate
• Cellular content
• Cause
• Typical sites
• Morphology

— Morphologic patterns of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Complete resolution is most likely when:

A. Injury is limited/short-lived with little tissue destruction
B. There is extensive tissue necrosis
C. Tissue cannot regenerate
D. Abundant fibrin cannot be cleared
cards.back:
A — Injury is limited/short-lived with little tissue destruction

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Resolution includes:

A. Removal of debris/microbes, resorption of edema, and regeneration
B. Only fibrosis
C. Only angiogenesis
D. Only chronic inflammation
cards.back:
A — Removal of debris/microbes, resorption of edema, and regeneration

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Edema fluid during resolution is resorbed principally by:

A. Lymphatics
B. Neutrophils
C. Fibroblasts
D. Platelets
cards.back:
A — Lymphatics

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Healing by fibrosis is particularly likely after:

A. Substantial tissue destruction
B. Minimal injury
C. Rapidly reversible injury
D. No tissue damage
cards.back:
A — Substantial tissue destruction

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Fibrosis also occurs when injured tissues:

A. Are incapable of regeneration
B. Regenerate perfectly
C. Have no extracellular matrix
D. Have no blood supply
cards.back:
A — Are incapable of regeneration

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Abundant fibrin exudation that cannot be adequately cleared can result in:

A. Organization/fibrosis
B. Immediate resolution
C. No tissue response
D. Only edema
cards.back:
A — Organization/fibrosis

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Acute inflammation progresses to chronic inflammation when:

A. The inflammatory response cannot be resolved
B. All stimuli disappear
C. Tissue regeneration is complete
D. Leukocytes undergo normal apoptosis
cards.back:
A — The inflammatory response cannot be resolved

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
According to Figure 3.17, causes that may lead into acute inflammation include:

A. Infarction, bacterial infection, toxins, trauma
B. Only autoimmunity
C. Only chronic infection
D. Only viral infection
cards.back:
A — Infarction, bacterial infection, toxins, trauma

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Causes leading to chronic inflammation in Figure 3.17 include:

A. Viral infection, chronic infection, persistent injury, autoimmune disease
B. Only trauma
C. Only infarction
D. Only toxins
cards.back:
A — Viral infection, chronic infection, persistent injury, autoimmune disease

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
The cardinal signs of inflammation result from:

A. Vascular and cellular reactions
B. Fibrosis only
C. Antibody production alone
D. Necrosis alone
cards.back:
A — Vascular and cellular reactions

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Pain in acute inflammation is associated with liberation of:

A. Prostaglandins, neuropeptides, and cytokines
B. Only complement
C. Only IgG
D. Only collagen
cards.back:
A — Prostaglandins, neuropeptides, and cytokines

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Loss of function results from:

A. Pain and tissue injury
B. Histamine alone
C. Edema alone
D. Fibrosis alone
cards.back:
A — Pain and tissue injury

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front: List the three outcomes of acute inflammation.
cards.back:
Complete resolution; healing by connective-tissue replacement/fibrosis; progression to chronic inflammation.

Key points:
• Resolution
• Fibrosis/organization
• Chronic inflammation
• Determined by severity and tissue regenerative capacity

— Outcomes and summary of acute inflammation

cards.front:
Chronic inflammation typically lasts:

A. Minutes
B. Hours only
C. Weeks or months
D. Seconds
cards.back:
C — Weeks or months

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Chronic inflammation is characterized by coexistence of:

A. Inflammation, tissue injury, and attempts at repair
B. Only inflammation
C. Only fibrosis
D. Only necrosis
cards.back:
A — Inflammation, tissue injury, and attempts at repair

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Chronic inflammation may begin:

A. Only after an acute episode
B. Insidiously as a low-grade smoldering response
C. Only after trauma
D. Only after bacterial infection
cards.back:
B — Insidiously as a low-grade smoldering response

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Persistent infections causing chronic inflammation are typically due to organisms:

A. Easy to eradicate
B. Difficult to eradicate
C. Unable to stimulate immunity
D. Restricted to blood
cards.back:
B — Difficult to eradicate

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Examples of persistent infectious agents include:

A. Mycobacteria, certain viruses, fungi, parasites
B. Only pyogenic cocci
C. Only viruses
D. Only fungi
cards.back:
A — Mycobacteria, certain viruses, fungi, parasites

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Persistent microorganisms may evoke:

A. Delayed-type hypersensitivity
B. Only immediate hypersensitivity
C. No immune response
D. Only antibody-independent immunity
cards.back:
A — Delayed-type hypersensitivity

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
An unresolved acute bacterial lung infection may progress to:

A. Chronic lung abscess
B. Serous blister
C. Granuloma necessarily
D. PNH
cards.back:
A — Chronic lung abscess

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis are examples of:

A. Chronic inflammation associated with autoimmunity
B. Acute bacterial disease
C. Purely infectious disease
D. Foreign-body granulomas
cards.back:
A — Chronic inflammation associated with autoimmunity

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Chronic inflammation due to excessive immune activation is called:

A. Hypersensitivity disease
B. Transudation
C. Resolution
D. Organization
cards.back:
A — Hypersensitivity disease

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Prolonged inhalation of particulate silica causes:

A. Silicosis
B. PNH
C. Gout
D. Asthma only
cards.back:
A — Silicosis

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Atherosclerosis is described here as a chronic inflammatory process driven at least partly by:

A. Tissue deposition of endogenous cholesterol and other lipids
B. Bacterial infection only
C. IgE only
D. Uric acid only
cards.back:
A — Tissue deposition of endogenous cholesterol and other lipids

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
The predominant inflammatory infiltrate in chronic inflammation consists of:

A. Neutrophils only
B. Mononuclear cells
C. Eosinophils only
D. Platelets
cards.back:
B — Mononuclear cells

— Chronic inflammation: definition, causes, and morphology

cards.front:
Mononuclear infiltrates include:

A. Macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells
B. Neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils
C. RBCs, platelets, neutrophils
D. Fibroblasts only
cards.back:
A — Macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells

cards.front: Describe the mechanism of fever.
cards.back:
Exogenous pyrogens such as LPS stimulate immune cells to release IL-1/TNF, which act on hypothalamic cells to increase COX activity and PGE₂ production. PGE₂ raises the hypothalamic temperature set point by reducing heat loss and increasing heat generation.

Key points:
• Exogenous pyrogens
• IL-1/TNF
• Hypothalamus
• COX
• PGE₂
• Increased set point

— Systemic effects of inflammation

cards.front: List important acute-phase proteins and their effects.
cards.back:
CRP, fibrinogen, and SAA are major acute-phase proteins. CRP/SAA can opsonize microbes and fix complement; fibrinogen produces rouleaux and contributes to ESR elevation; persistent SAA elevation may produce secondary amyloidosis.

Key points:
• CRP
• Fibrinogen
• SAA
• Opsonization/complement
• ESR
• Amyloidosis

— Systemic effects of inflammation

cards.front: Describe leukocytosis in acute inflammation.
cards.back:
Cytokines stimulate rapid bone-marrow release of granulocytes, causing neutrophilia and a shift to the left; prolonged infection increases precursor proliferation through CSFs.

• Bone marrow release
• Mature + immature neutrophils
• Left shift
• CSFs
• Prolonged infection

— Systemic effects of inflammation

cards.front: Describe septic shock as presented in Robbins.
cards.back:
Severe bacterial infection produces very high TNF/IL-1 and other cytokine levels, resulting in hypotension, DIC, insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, and other metabolic disturbances.

Key points:
• Sepsis
• TNF/IL-1
• Hypotension
• DIC
• Metabolic disturbance
• SIRS

— Systemic effects of inflammation
