A. Fibroblast migration/proliferation followed by ECM deposition
B. Neutrophil migration followed by NET formation
C. Angiogenesis followed by phagocytosis
D. Fibrosis followed by inflammation
cards.back:
A — Fibroblast migration/proliferation followed by ECM deposition

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Important locally produced growth factors regulating fibroblast proliferation include:

A. PDGF, FGF-2, TGF-β
B. C3a, C3b, C5a
C. IgG, IgE, IgA
D. Histamine, serotonin, bradykinin
cards.back:
A — PDGF, FGF-2, TGF-β

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
The most important cytokine for synthesis and deposition of connective-tissue proteins is:

A. IL-1
B. TGF-β
C. TNF
D. IL-17
cards.back:
B — TGF-β

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TGF-β is produced by:

A. Most cells in granulation tissue, including M2 macrophages
B. Only hepatocytes
C. Only neutrophils
D. Only endothelial cells
cards.back:
A — Most cells in granulation tissue, including M2 macrophages

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Tissue TGF-β levels are regulated mainly by:

A. Transcription alone
B. Posttranscriptional activation of latent TGF-β, secretion of active TGF-β, and ECM interactions
C. Histamine release
D. Complement activation
cards.back:
B — Posttranscriptional activation of latent TGF-β, secretion of active TGF-β, and ECM interactions

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TGF-β stimulates:

A. Fibroblast migration and proliferation
B. Only neutrophil apoptosis
C. Platelet aggregation
D. Leukocyte rolling
cards.back:
A — Fibroblast migration and proliferation

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TGF-β increases synthesis of:

A. Collagen and fibronectin
B. Histamine and serotonin
C. C3a and C5a
D. IgE and IgG
cards.back:
A — Collagen and fibronectin

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TGF-β decreases ECM degradation by:

A. Activating metalloproteinases
B. Inhibiting metalloproteinases
C. Activating neutrophils
D. Inhibiting collagen synthesis
cards.back:
B — Inhibiting metalloproteinases

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TGF-β contributes to fibrosis in:

A. Lung, liver, and kidneys
B. Brain only
C. Bone marrow only
D. Skin only
cards.back:
A — Lung, liver, and kidneys

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TGF-β is paradoxically also:

A. A proinflammatory cytokine only
B. An antiinflammatory cytokine
C. A chemokine
D. A complement protein
cards.back:
B — An antiinflammatory cytokine

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TGF-β limits inflammation partly by inhibiting:

A. Lymphocyte proliferation and other leukocyte activity
B. Collagen synthesis
C. Fibroblast migration
D. Angiogenesis exclusively
cards.back:
A — Lymphocyte proliferation and other leukocyte activity

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
As a scar matures, vascularity generally:

A. Increases continuously
B. Regresses
C. Remains identical to granulation tissue
D. Disappears immediately
cards.back:
B — Regresses

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
A mature scar is typically:

A. Pale and largely avascular
B. Bright red and highly vascular
C. Edematous
D. Neutrophil-rich
cards.back:
A — Pale and largely avascular

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Fibroblasts that acquire smooth-muscle-like contractile properties are called:

A. Myofibroblasts
B. Fibrocytes
C. Epithelioid cells
D. Pericytes
cards.back:
A — Myofibroblasts

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Myofibroblasts contribute to:

A. Scar contraction
B. Fever
C. Phagocytosis
D. Complement activation
cards.back:
A — Scar contraction

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
MMP activity is dependent on:

A. Metal ions such as zinc
B. Calcium only
C. Sodium only
D. Histamine
cards.back:
A — Metal ions such as zinc

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Interstitial collagenases include:

A. MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-3
B. MMP-5, MMP-6, MMP-7
C. COX-1, COX-2, iNOS
D. TIMP-1, TIMP-2, TIMP-3
cards.back:
A — MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-3

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Interstitial collagenases degrade:

A. Fibrillar collagen
B. Histamine
C. Fibrin only
D. DNA
cards.back:
A — Fibrillar collagen

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Gelatinases degrade:

A. Amorphous collagen and fibronectin
B. Only fibrillar collagen
C. Complement proteins only
D. DNA only
cards.back:
A — Amorphous collagen and fibronectin

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Stromelysins degrade:

A. Proteoglycans, laminin, fibronectin, and amorphous collagen
B. Only fibrillar collagen
C. Only fibrin
D. Only elastin
cards.back:
A — Proteoglycans, laminin, fibronectin, and amorphous collagen

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
MMPs are produced by:

A. Fibroblasts, macrophages, neutrophils, synovial cells, and some epithelial cells
B. Only fibroblasts
C. Only macrophages
D. Only neutrophils
cards.back:
A — Fibroblasts, macrophages, neutrophils, synovial cells, and some epithelial cells

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
MMPs are synthesized as:

A. Active enzymes
B. Inactive zymogens
C. Cytokines
D. Opsonins
cards.back:
B — Inactive zymogens

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
MMP activation can be accomplished by:

A. Proteases such as plasmin
B. Histamine
C. IgG
D. TNF exclusively
cards.back:
A — Proteases such as plasmin

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
Activated collagenases can be inhibited by:

A. TIMPs
B. TLRs
C. Selectins
D. Complement
cards.back:
A — TIMPs

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
TIMPs are produced by:

A. Most mesenchymal cells
B. Only neutrophils
C. Only endothelial cells
D. Only platelets
cards.back:
A — Most mesenchymal cells

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front: Explain the role of TGF-β in tissue repair.
cards.back:
TGF-β promotes fibroblast migration/proliferation, collagen and fibronectin synthesis, inhibits ECM degradation, promotes fibrosis, and also suppresses inflammatory lymphocyte/leukocyte activity.

Key points:
• Fibroblasts
• Collagen
• Fibronectin
• MMP inhibition
• Fibrosis
• Anti-inflammatory effect

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front: Describe the MMP–TIMP system in scar remodeling.
cards.back:
MMPs degrade collagen and other ECM components and are produced as inactive zymogens activated by injury-associated proteases. TIMPs subsequently inhibit activated MMPs, controlling ECM remodeling.

Key points:
• MMPs
• Metal-dependent enzymes
• Zymogens
• Plasmin
• ECM degradation
• TIMPs

— Connective-tissue deposition and remodeling

cards.front:
The clinically most important cause of delayed wound healing is:

A. Infection
B. Mild edema
C. Fever
D. Leukocytosis
cards.back:
A — Infection

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Infection delays healing partly by:

A. Prolonging inflammation and increasing local tissue injury
B. Increasing collagen synthesis
C. Preventing leukocyte recruitment
D. Increasing tissue oxygenation
cards.back:
A — Prolonging inflammation and increasing local tissue injury

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
An important systemic cause of abnormal wound healing is:

A. Diabetes
B. Asthma
C. Migraine
D. Hyperthyroidism
cards.back:
A — Diabetes

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Deficiency of which nutrients inhibits collagen synthesis?

A. Protein and vitamin C
B. Vitamin B12 and folate only
C. Iron and calcium only
D. Vitamin D only
cards.back:
A — Protein and vitamin C

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Glucocorticoids can weaken scars by:

A. Increasing TGF-β
B. Inhibiting TGF-β production and diminishing fibrosis
C. Increasing collagen synthesis
D. Increasing fibroblast proliferation
cards.back:
B — Inhibiting TGF-β production and diminishing fibrosis

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Glucocorticoid inhibition of repair can sometimes be desirable in:

A. Corneal infections
B. Bone fractures
C. Abdominal wound dehiscence
D. Diabetic ulcers
cards.back:
A — Corneal infections

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Increased local pressure or torsion can cause:

A. Wound dehiscence
B. Granuloma formation
C. Eosinophilia
D. Angiogenesis
cards.back:
A — Wound dehiscence

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Poor perfusion can be caused by:

A. Peripheral vascular disease, arteriosclerosis, diabetes, or obstructed venous drainage
B. Only infection
C. Only anemia
D. Only hypotension
cards.back:
A — Peripheral vascular disease, arteriosclerosis, diabetes, or obstructed venous drainage

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Foreign bodies delay healing by:

A. Perpetuating chronic inflammation
B. Increasing epithelial regeneration
C. Increasing oxygen delivery
D. Decreasing fibrosis
cards.back:
A — Perpetuating chronic inflammation

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Fragments of all of the following are listed as potentially impairing healing EXCEPT:

A. Steel
B. Glass
C. Bone
D. Albumin
cards.back:
D — Albumin

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Complete restoration is possible only in tissues composed of:

A. Permanent cells only
B. Stable and labile cells
C. Neurons only
D. Cardiac myocytes only
cards.back:
B — Stable and labile cells

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Injury to tissues composed of permanent cells generally results in:

A. Complete regeneration
B. Scarring and some loss of function
C. No repair
D. Only edema
cards.back:
B — Scarring and some loss of function

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
In pleural, peritoneal, or synovial spaces, extensive exudates can undergo:

A. Digestion and resorption
B. Immediate fibrosis in every case
C. Caseation
D. Granuloma formation
cards.back:
A — Digestion and resorption

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Proteolytic digestion of exudate in these spaces is initiated by:

A. Leukocyte proteolytic enzymes
B. Platelets
C. Fibroblasts
D. RBCs
cards.back:
A — Leukocyte proteolytic enzymes

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
In the absence of cellular necrosis, resolution of an exudate generally leads to:

A. Restoration of normal tissue architecture
B. Permanent fibrosis
C. Granuloma formation
D. Keloid formation
cards.back:
A — Restoration of normal tissue architecture

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Larger accumulations of exudate may lead to:

A. Granulation tissue ingrowth and organization
B. Immediate resolution
C. Pure regeneration
D. No repair response
cards.back:
A — Granulation tissue ingrowth and organization

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front: List major factors that impair tissue repair.
cards.back:
Infection, diabetes, protein/vitamin C deficiency, glucocorticoids, mechanical stress, poor perfusion, foreign bodies, tissue type/extent of injury, and location of injury.

Key points:
• Infection
• Diabetes
• Nutrition
• Steroids
• Perfusion
• Mechanical factors
• Foreign bodies
• Tissue characteristics

— Factors influencing tissue repair

cards.front:
Healing by first intention is also called:

A. Secondary union
B. Primary union
C. Organization
D. Fibrosis
cards.back:
B — Primary union

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
First-intention healing occurs when the injury:

A. Involves only the epithelial layer or is a clean, closely approximated incision
B. Produces massive tissue loss
C. Produces an abscess
D. Involves permanent tissues exclusively
cards.back:
A — Involves only the epithelial layer or is a clean, closely approximated incision

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
A typical example of first-intention healing is:

A. Clean uninfected surgical incision closed with sutures
B. Large pressure ulcer
C. Diabetic foot ulcer
D. Chronic osteomyelitis
cards.back:
A — Clean uninfected surgical incision closed with sutures

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
First-intention healing causes:

A. Extensive tissue loss
B. Focal basement-membrane disruption and death of relatively few cells
C. Massive necrosis
D. Extensive granulation tissue
cards.back:
B — Focal basement-membrane disruption and death of relatively few cells

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
The three connected processes of wound repair include:

A. Inflammation, proliferation, maturation
B. Necrosis, caseation, fibrosis
C. Vasoconstriction, thrombosis, granuloma formation
D. Opsonization, phagocytosis, fever
cards.back:
A — Inflammation, proliferation, maturation

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
Immediately after wounding, coagulation results in:

A. Blood-clot formation
B. Granuloma formation
C. Fibrosis
D. Angiogenesis
cards.back:
A — Blood-clot formation

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
The wound clot primarily:

A. Stops bleeding and supports migrating cells
B. Causes tissue necrosis
C. Prevents epithelial migration
D. Prevents fibroblast recruitment
cards.back:
A — Stops bleeding and supports migrating cells

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
Migrating cells are attracted partly by:

A. Growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines
B. Only collagen
C. Only histamine
D. Only complement
cards.back:
A — Growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
Within 24 hours of a clean incision, which cells are seen at the incision margin?

A. Neutrophils
B. Plasma cells
C. Eosinophils
D. Fibroblasts only
cards.back:
A — Neutrophils

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
Within 24–48 hours, epithelial cells:

A. Begin migrating and proliferating along the dermis
B. Become macrophages
C. Undergo apoptosis
D. Form granulation tissue
cards.back:
A — Begin migrating and proliferating along the dermis

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
The epithelial layer formed within 24–48 hours is:

A. Thick and keratinized immediately
B. Thin but continuous
C. Absent
D. Composed of fibroblasts
cards.back:
B — Thin but continuous

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
By day 3, neutrophils are largely replaced by:

A. Macrophages
B. Eosinophils
C. Plasma cells
D. Fibroblasts
cards.back:
A — Macrophages

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
By day 3, macrophages help by:

A. Clearing debris/fibrin and promoting angiogenesis and ECM deposition
B. Destroying all fibroblasts
C. Blocking vascular growth
D. Preventing granulation tissue formation
cards.back:
A — Clearing debris/fibrin and promoting angiogenesis and ECM deposition

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
By approximately day 5:

A. Neovascularization reaches its peak
B. Neutrophils peak
C. Fibrosis is complete
D. Scar is fully mature
cards.back:
A — Neovascularization reaches its peak

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
New vessels in granulation tissue are:

A. Nonpermeable
B. Leaky
C. Absent
D. Fully mature immediately
cards.back:
B — Leaky

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
During the second week:

A. Collagen accumulation and fibroblast proliferation continue
B. Leukocyte infiltration increases dramatically
C. Vascularity increases indefinitely
D. The wound becomes an abscess
cards.back:
A — Collagen accumulation and fibroblast proliferation continue

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
During the second week, which decreases substantially?

A. Leukocyte infiltrate, edema, and vascularity
B. Collagen
C. Fibroblasts
D. Epithelial continuity
cards.back:
A — Leukocyte infiltrate, edema, and vascularity

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
By the end of the first month, the scar consists largely of:

A. Cellular connective tissue with few inflammatory cells and essentially normal epidermis
B. Dense neutrophils
C. Purulent material
D. Granulation tissue with maximal vascularity
cards.back:
A — Cellular connective tissue with few inflammatory cells and essentially normal epidermis

— Healing by first intention

cards.front: Describe healing by first intention chronologically.
cards.back:
A clot forms immediately; neutrophils appear within 24 h; epithelial cells migrate by 24–48 h; macrophages replace neutrophils and granulation tissue develops by day 3; neovascularization peaks by day 5; collagen accumulates during the second week; by one month a relatively cellular scar with normal epidermis remains.

Key points:
• 24 h
• 24–48 h
• Day 3
• Day 5
• Second week
• First month

— Healing by first intention

cards.front:
Healing by second intention is also called:

A. Primary union
B. Secondary union
C. Organization only
D. Regeneration only
cards.back:
B — Secondary union

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Compared with first intention, second-intention wounds have:

A. Smaller clot and less inflammation
B. Larger clot, more exudate, and more necrotic debris
C. Less granulation tissue
D. No wound contraction
cards.back:
B — Larger clot, more exudate, and more necrotic debris

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Inflammation is more intense in second intention primarily because:

A. There is more necrotic debris, exudate, and fibrin to remove
B. There are fewer leukocytes
C. There is no clot
D. There is no tissue injury
cards.back:
A — There is more necrotic debris, exudate, and fibrin to remove

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Second-intention wounds generate:

A. Less granulation tissue than first-intention wounds
B. Much larger amounts of granulation tissue
C. No fibroblasts
D. No vascular proliferation
cards.back:
B — Much larger amounts of granulation tissue

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Greater granulation tissue generally produces:

A. A greater scar mass
B. Less scar
C. No scar
D. Complete regeneration
cards.back:
A — A greater scar mass

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
The initial provisional matrix in second-intention healing contains:

A. Fibrin, plasma fibronectin, and type III collagen
B. Only type I collagen
C. Only elastin
D. Only laminin
cards.back:
A — Fibrin, plasma fibronectin, and type III collagen

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
By approximately 2 weeks, the provisional matrix is replaced mainly by:

A. Type I collagen
B. Type II collagen
C. Elastin
D. Fibrin
cards.back:
A — Type I collagen

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Ultimately the original granulation-tissue scaffold becomes:

A. A pale, avascular scar
B. A highly vascular tissue
C. A granuloma
D. A pus-filled cavity
cards.back:
A — A pale, avascular scar

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Destroyed dermal appendages within a second-intention wound:

A. Regenerate completely
B. Are permanently lost
C. Become macrophages
D. Become blood vessels
cards.back:
B — Are permanently lost

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Wound contraction is especially important in:

A. Secondary intention
B. Primary intention only
C. Granuloma formation
D. Serous inflammation
cards.back:
A — Secondary intention

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Wound contraction reduces:

A. The gap between dermal edges and wound surface area
B. Blood flow
C. Collagen synthesis
D. Epithelial migration
cards.back:
A — The gap between dermal edges and wound surface area

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Wound contraction depends largely on:

A. Myofibroblasts
B. Neutrophils
C. Eosinophils
D. Plasma cells
cards.back:
A — Myofibroblasts

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Within 6 weeks, large skin defects may be reduced to approximately:

A. 50%–60% of original size
B. 5%–10% of original size
C. 80%–90%
D. 1%
cards.back:
B — 5%–10%

— Healing by second intention

cards.front: Compare first- and second-intention healing.
cards.back:
Second intention occurs with large tissue defects, produces more inflammation, granulation tissue and scarring, and exhibits marked wound contraction; first intention occurs with closely approximated clean wounds and has less tissue loss, granulation tissue, and contraction.

Key points:
• Wound size
• Inflammation
• Granulation tissue
• Scar
• Contraction

— Healing by second intention

cards.front:
Carefully sutured wounds initially have approximately:

A. 10% of normal strength
B. 30%
C. 70%
D. 100%
cards.back:
C — 70%

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
The initial wound strength of sutured wounds is largely due to:

A. Sutures themselves
B. Mature collagen
C. Angiogenesis
D. Granulation tissue
cards.back:
A — Sutures themselves

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
Increased tensile strength during the first two months results from:

A. Excess collagen synthesis over degradation, collagen cross-linking, and increased fiber size
B. Reduced collagen synthesis
C. Increased neutrophils
D. Increased edema
cards.back:
A — Excess collagen synthesis over degradation, collagen cross-linking, and increased fiber size

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
By about 3 months, wound strength reaches approximately:

A. 20%–30%
B. 40%–50%
C. 70%–80%
D. 100%
cards.back:
C — 70%–80%

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
After approximately 3 months, wound strength:

A. Usually does not substantially improve further
B. Immediately falls to zero
C. Reaches 150% of normal
D. Doubles every month
cards.back:
A — Usually does not substantially improve further

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
Fibrosis refers to:

A. Excessive deposition of collagen and other ECM components in tissue
B. Complete tissue regeneration
C. Leukocyte recruitment
D. Edema only
cards.back:
A — Excessive deposition of collagen and other ECM components in tissue

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
Fibrosis can cause:

A. Substantial organ dysfunction and organ failure
B. Only cosmetic change
C. Only fever
D. Only leukocytosis
cards.back:
A — Substantial organ dysfunction and organ failure

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
Which is listed as a fibrotic disorder?

A. Liver cirrhosis
B. Constrictive pericarditis
C. End-stage kidney disease
D. All of the above
cards.back:
D — All of the above

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is classified as:

A. A fibrosing disease of the lung
B. An acute suppurative process
C. A granulomatous disease only
D. A skin disorder
cards.back:
A — A fibrosing disease of the lung

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front: Describe the evolution of wound tensile strength.
cards.back:
Sutured wounds initially possess about 70% of normal strength because of sutures. Collagen synthesis and cross-linking increase tensile strength during the first two months; by 3 months strength reaches about 70–80% of normal and then generally plateaus.

Key points:
• 70% initially
• Sutures
• Collagen synthesis
• Cross-linking
• 70–80% at 3 months
• Plateau

— Wound strength and fibrosis

cards.front:
Venous leg ulcers occur most commonly because of:

A. Chronic venous hypertension
B. Arterial thrombosis only
C. Autoimmune disease
D. Acute infection
cards.back:
A — Chronic venous hypertension

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Chronic venous hypertension may result from:

A. Severe varicose veins or congestive heart failure
B. Asthma
C. Hepatitis
D. Hyperthyroidism
cards.back:
A — Severe varicose veins or congestive heart failure

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Hemosiderin deposits in venous ulcers result from:

A. RBC breakdown
B. Collagen synthesis
C. Platelet aggregation
D. Eosinophil degranulation
cards.back:
A — RBC breakdown

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Venous leg ulcers fail to heal partly because of:

A. Poor oxygen delivery
B. Excess collagen
C. Excess epithelial migration
D. Excess blood flow
cards.back:
A — Poor oxygen delivery

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Arterial ulcers are associated especially with:

A. Peripheral arterial atherosclerosis and diabetes
B. Chronic venous hypertension
C. Helminth infection
D. Asthma
cards.back:
A — Peripheral arterial atherosclerosis and diabetes

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Arterial-ulcer ischemia initially produces:

A. Atrophy followed by necrosis
B. Hypertrophy followed by fibrosis
C. Hyperplasia followed by edema
D. Granuloma formation
cards.back:
A — Atrophy followed by necrosis

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Arterial ulcers can be:

A. Quite painful
B. Always painless
C. Always pruritic
D. Always infected
cards.back:
A — Quite painful

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Diabetic ulcers most commonly affect:

A. Lower extremities, particularly feet
B. Face
C. Upper arm
D. Scalp
cards.back:
A — Lower extremities, particularly feet

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Diabetic ulcer healing is impaired by all of the following EXCEPT:

A. Vascular disease/ischemia
B. Neuropathy
C. Systemic metabolic abnormalities
D. Increased tissue oxygenation
cards.back:
D — Increased tissue oxygenation

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Secondary infection in diabetic ulcers:

A. May contribute to failure to heal
B. Always accelerates healing
C. Prevents necrosis
D. Has no effect
cards.back:
A — May contribute to failure to heal

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Histologically, diabetic ulcers show:

A. Epithelial ulceration and extensive granulation tissue in underlying dermis
B. Only caseation
C. Only fibrosis
D. Only eosinophils
cards.back:
A — Epithelial ulceration and extensive granulation tissue in underlying dermis

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Pressure sores result from:

A. Prolonged compression against bone with local ischemia
B. Excessive arterial flow
C. Viral infection
D. Autoimmunity
cards.back:
A — Prolonged compression against bone with local ischemia

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Pressure sores are particularly associated with:

A. Elderly, immobile patients with multiple morbidities
B. Healthy young athletes
C. Hyperthyroidism
D. Acute viral infections
cards.back:
A — Elderly, immobile patients with multiple morbidities

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Internal or external reopening of a surgical incision is called:

A. Dehiscence
B. Organization
C. Keloid
D. Contracture
cards.back:
A — Dehiscence

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Risk factors for wound dehiscence include:

A. Obesity, malnutrition, infection, vascular insufficiency
B. Only fever
C. Only neutrophilia
D. Only diabetes
cards.back:
A — Obesity, malnutrition, infection, vascular insufficiency

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front:
Abdominal wound dehiscence can be precipitated by:

A. Vomiting and coughing
B. Walking
C. Sleeping
D. Eating
cards.back:
A — Vomiting and coughing

— Defects in healing: chronic wounds

cards.front: Differentiate venous, arterial, diabetic, and pressure ulcers.
cards.back:
• Venous: chronic venous hypertension, poor oxygen delivery, hemosiderin • Arterial: atherosclerotic ischemia, atrophy → necrosis, pain • Diabetic: ischemia + neuropathy + metabolic abnormalities + infection; commonly feet • Pressure: prolonged compression and local ischemia
